title: Validation of linux capabilities in container security context should be stricter
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Validation for capabilities added to the security context of containers should be improved to make it easier to schedule containers with the expected capabilities.

/sig apps

OPTION 1: `CAP_`/`cap_` prefix is be forbidden
- example capabilities that would be allowed:
	- `SYS_ADMIN` (uppercase capability)
	- `sys_admin` (lowercase capability)
	- `INVALID_CAPABILITY` (non-existent capability, without forbidden prefix)
- example capabilities that would be rejected:
	- `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`
	- `cap_sys_admin`

OPTION 2: Only capabilities from a select list of capabilities should be allowed, in both upper- and lowercase
- example capabilities that would be allowed:
	- `SYS_ADMIN` (uppercase capability)
	- `sys_admin` (lowercase capability)
- example capabilities that would be rejected:
	- `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`
	- `cap_sys_admin`
	- `INVALID_CAPABILITY` (non-existent capability)
	- ...

In my opinion Option 2 is preferred, since it will only allow scheduling of containers, that receive the expected capability.

ℹ️ Open to create a PR if this proposal is accepted. I'd also like to take this opportunity to improve capability validation, so it's no longer required to define the string in each location, but have a case insensitive check somewhere.

### Why is this needed?

⚠️ Currently only uppercase capabilities are validated correctly in the security context, while lowercase capabilities add the same capability to the container.

The following pod manifest was used to create containers with specific capabilities added and then the current capabilities of the created container were logged using `capsh --print`:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine
    command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add -U libcap && capsh --print']
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - "ALL"
        add:
        - "SYS_ADMIN"
        # - "sys_admin"
        # - "cap_sys_admin"
        # - "CAP_SYS_ADMIN"
        # - "INVALID_CAPABILITY"
```


<details>
<summary>Example output from pod with `SYS_ADMIN` capability</summary>

```console
...
Current: cap_sys_admin=ep
Bounding set =cap_sys_admin
Ambient set =
Current IAB: !cap_chown,!cap_dac_override,!cap_dac_read_search,!cap_fowner,!cap_fsetid,!cap_kill,!cap_setgid,!cap_setuid,!cap_setpcap,!cap_linux_immutable,!cap_net_bind_service,!cap_net_broadcast,!cap_net_adm
Securebits: 00/0x0/1'b0 (no-new-privs=0)
 secure-noroot: no (unlocked)
 secure-no-suid-fixup: no (unlocked)
 secure-keep-caps: no (unlocked)
 secure-no-ambient-raise: no (unlocked)
uid=0(root) euid=0(root)
gid=0(root)
groups=0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),3(sys),4(adm),6(disk),10(wheel),11(floppy),20(dialout),26(tape),27(video)
Guessed mode: HYBRID (4)
```

`Current: cap_sys_admin=ep` indicates that the `SYS_ADMIN` capability was successfully added to the container.

</details>

Result of adding different capabilities to the container's security context:
- ✅ `SYS_ADMIN`: container has expected `cap_sys_admin` capability
- ✅ `sys_admin`: container has expected `cap_sys_admin` capability
- ❌ `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`: container missing expected `cap_sys_admin` capability
- ❌ `cap_sys_admin`: container missing expected `cap_sys_admin` capability
- ❌ `INVALID_CAPABILITY`: container scheduled with invalid capability (unknown/invalid capability)

title: Terraform Plugins stored in Persistent Volume are loaded into pod memory during execution
body:
### What happened?
Tested this issue on Google Kubernetes Engine and minikube setup.
In **Google Kubernetes Engine(GKE)**

1. Executing terraform init, terraform plan, terraform apply, terraform destroy commands in kubernetes pod. 
2. Cache directory is created in Persistent Volume for storing the terraform plugins.
3. Plugins/Binaries downloaded during terraform execution are stored in Persistent Volume but they are getting loaded into pod memory(occupying RAM).
4. Even after terraform execution is completed plugins are not getting cleared from pod memory.(The occupied memory is not getting cleared)
5. We are using PV especially to store terraform plugins instead of downloading them into pod but even then they are getting  copied into pod memory while terraform execution.

Example : While provisioning the AWS terraform template, we are caching the plugins using "TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR", the plugin with size of 400MB is getting downloaded in the specified cache directory(Cache directory path is inside the pod but it is mounted to an external storage using persistent volume(PV)) when terraform init is performed.In this case it is not occupying any pod memory as we have mounted the plugin-cache directory path to an external storage.But when we perform terraform plan, terraform apply, terraform destroy those plugins from the cache directory are getting loaded into the pod-memory results in the occupying of additional 400MB space.

6. The occupied memory is getting cleared only after removing the plugins from the plugin-cache directory.
Note: We are using external storage (Persistent Volume) to store the plugin-cache, they are not getting stored inside the pod.

**In Minikube setup**

1. Executing terraform init, terraform plan, terraform apply, terraform destroy commands in kubernetes pod. And cache directory is created in Persistent Volume for storing the terraform plugins.
2. Plugins/Binaries downloaded during terraform execution are stored in Persistent Volume which is mounted to path in kubernetes pod but while executing of terraform commands ,plugins are also loaded into pod memory.
3. Even after execution is completed the loaded plugins are not getting cleared from the pod memory.(The occupied memory is not getting cleared)
4. But once we delete the pod and run terraform commands now terraform plugins are not getting loaded into memory.Plugins are directly used from cache.

**Important**: When terraform plugins are added during pod runtime, they are getting loaded into pod memory. But once pod is deleted and plugin is available in cache directory before pod start, now if we execute terraform commands plugins are not getting loaded into memory.This is happening in minikube setup, but in GKE cluster in both the scenarios (during runtime and after pod start) plugins are loaded into pod memory.

Minikube Kubernetes Version

Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.4", GitCommit:"e6c093d87ea4cbb530a7b2ae91e54c0842d8308a", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-02-16T12:38:05Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.7", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/30903879/590fcd6c-31be-41ea-911a-4ccd20f81faa)



### What did you expect to happen?

1. We are running the terraform commands inside a Kubernetes pod with Linux environment.
2. Plugins/Binaries downloaded during terraform execution are stored in Persistent Volume
3. When terraform init, terraform plan, terraform apply are executed inside a Kubernetes pod, plugins should be stored and used from Persistent Volume but should not be loaded into pod memory.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Set up a Kubernetes cluster containing a pod with linux_amd64 and GO installed inside it.
2. Create a plugin cache dir (TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR) inside a pod for storing the plugins.
3. Create a Persistence Volume with an external storage and mount it to plugin cache dir inside the pod.
8. Perform terraform init, terraform plan, terraform apply, terraform destroy to any terraform template (AWS for example)

title: Pod volume configuration miss match between config map and secrets
body:
### What happened?

Configuration of specifying the `ConfigMap` and `Secret` as a volume for `Pod` are not consistent with each other.
In K8S Pod key to specify a `ConfigMap` in volumes is `name`, but key to specify a `Secret`  name is `secretName`. 

As all the other configuration to set a volume as ConfigMap and Secret are same, the key name should be same as well to avoid confusion. 


### What did you expect to happen?

While setting the `Secret` as volume in `Pod`, change the key of Secret to `name` from `secretName`

AS IS:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: secret-vol
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: secret-vol 
      secret:
         secretName: test-secret
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: nginx
```

TO BE:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: secret-vol
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: secret-vol 
      secret:
         name: test-secret
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: nginx
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod with `Secret` as volume.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: secret-vol
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: secret-vol
      secret:
         secretName: test-secret
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: nginx
```

title: Paginate initial list inside the storage watcher
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add pagination to the initial list that is performed by the etcd watcher.

We do not paginate the list when we do not set RV here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a005617111cc44caa6c6cc4ecfcc3d4a0d30d008/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L253-L263

as we do not add any limit to `OpOption` in the `sync()` method:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a005617111cc44caa6c6cc4ecfcc3d4a0d30d008/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L222-L230

### Why is this needed?

gRPC has an upper limit for response size up to 2^31-1 ~ 2 GB which might be too small if:

1. Some K8s API client initiates a watch request directly to etcd rather than using watch cache,
2. Total size of requested resources exceed that limit, resulting in an error in this fashion from etcd:

```
failed to sync with latest state: rpc error: code = ResourceExhausted desc = grpc: trying to send message larger than max (2148646892 vs. 2147483647)
```

hence resulting in inability to initiate a watch request by that particular K8s API client.

title: CVE-2023-3893: Insufficient input sanitization on kubernetes-csi-proxy leads to privilege escalation
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/av:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) - **HIGH** (8.8)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where a user that can create pods on Windows nodes running kubernetes-csi-proxy may be able to escalate to admin privileges on those nodes. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if they include Windows nodes running kubernetes-csi-proxy.

### Am I vulnerable?

Any kubernetes environment with Windows nodes that are running kubernetes-csi-proxy is impacted.  This is a common default configuration on Windows nodes.  Run `kubectl get nodes -l kubernetes.io/os=windows` to see if any Windows nodes are in use.

#### Affected Versions

- kubernetes-csi-proxy <= v2.0.0-alpha.0
- kubernetes-csi-proxy <= v1.1.2

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

The provided patch fully mitigates the vulnerability and has no known side effects.  Full mitigation for this class of issues requires patches applied for CVE-2023-3676, CVE-2023-3955, and CVE-2023-3893.

Outside of applying the provided patch, there are no known mitigations to this vulnerability.

#### Fixed Versions

- kubernetes-csi-proxy master - fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/pull/306
- kubernetes-csi-proxy v2.0.0-alpha.1 - fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/pull/307
- kubernetes-csi-proxy v1.1.3 - fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/pull/306

To upgrade: cordon the node, stop the associated Windows service, replace the csi-proxy.exe binary, restart the associated Windows service, and un-cordon the node.  See the installation docs for more details: https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy#installation

If a Windows host process daemon set is used to run kubernetes-csi-proxy such as https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-driver-smb/blob/master/charts/latest/csi-driver-smb/templates/csi-proxy-windows.yaml, simply upgrade the image to a fixed version such as ghcr.io/kubernetes-sigs/sig-windows/csi-proxy:v1.1.3

### Detection

Kubernetes audit logs can be used to detect if this vulnerability is being exploited. Pod create events with embedded powershell commands are a strong indication of exploitation.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

This vulnerability was discovered by James Sturtevant @jsturtevant and Mark Rossetti @marosset during the process of fixing CVE-2023-3676 (that original CVE was reported by Tomer Peled @tomerpeled92)

title: Kubelet cannot finish terminating a pod that uses a PVC with volumeMode: Block when poweroff the node and then restarting the node
body:
### What happened?

A pod uses a PVC with volumeMode: Block. The block volume is backed by a block device on the node (which is created by some CSI storage providers).  If the node operating system is powered off , if the user delete the pod or the pod be eviceted by kcm, And then restarting the node, The pod would be stuck in terminating forever since Kubelet refuses to UnmapBlockVolume. kubelet  cannot delete the pod successfully.  

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should be able to finish terminating a pod  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.Install a CSI storage provider that supports volumeMode: Block.

2.Deloy a pod that has volumeClaimTemplates with volumeMode: Block. 

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-pod
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-pod
      name: test-pod
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx:1.17.9
        name: test
        volumeDevices:
        - devicePath: /dev/blk-vol-1
          name: blk-vol-1
        volumeMounts:
      volumes:
      - name: blk-vol-1
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: test-bv
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: test-bv
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes: [ "ReadWriteMany" ]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
  storageClassName: FILLIN
  volumeMode: Block
```
3.After pod is running ,to  power off the node
4.delete the po: kubectl delete po test-pod
5.restart the node

The pod is stuck in terminating state forever. Logs from kubelet:

title: User can easily crash an entire cluster by creating pod with memory-backed EmptyDir
body:
### What happened?

**The following phenomena were observed:**
* Pods that mounts a memory-backed EmptyDir with a default size (allocatable) was created on the node, and the app ran that quickly consumes this EmptyDir.
* Since it is not counted as memory usage unless EmptyDir is actually consumed, multiple such Pods can be created on the same node.
* Naturally, multiple tmpfs with approximately the same capacity as the node's memory size are also created.
  + This causes memory overcommited situation.
* Multiple EmptyDirs were consumed fast enough, then K8s tried to delete Pods and EmptyDirs due to excessive memory usage.
  + Pod status becomes OOMKilled
  + Other attempts to deploy pods (nginx) are not scheduled
* The deletion of tmpfs could not do in time, so the moment of memory exhaustion came and the node crashed.
  + If the number of replicas in a Deployment is set to be sufficiently higher, all schedulable nodes crashed.
  + Pod status becomes ContainerStatusUnknown
  + Pod status is Terminating but not deleted
  + The memory backed tmpfs on node is no longer deleted
  + The node becomes NotReady and you can't even log in with SSH
  + _**This could be a security issue...**_

**Operations and logs**
* kubelet log ([deployment-memvol-replica-6.log](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/12250107/deployment-memvol-replica-6.log))
  + 10:08 Worker VMs were restarted
  + Deploy `memvol` deployment with 6 replicas.
  + Each worker has two pods deployed
  + The Pods kept the Running state for about 5 minutes
, although they consumed most of the memory and CPU.
  + The node seems to be NotReady, so I deleted the deployment.
  + Stopped the worker VMs because the Pod remained in Terminating state.
  + Start worker VMs again.

### What did you expect to happen?

* Memory usage by EmptyDir should be strictry managed by k8s
  + Memory overcommit should be allowed by cluster admin, not by default.
  + Or enable to be controlled the total size of memory-backed EmptyDir per worker node.
  + Add taint to node for that memory-overcommit-allowed or memory-backed-emptydir-allowed.
* The default size of memory-backed EmptiDir should be smaller size that is less likely to cause problems.
  + e.g. 50Mi.

I hope that the cluster admins can prevent such situations where this kind of phenomenon can easily occur, whether due to a mistake or malicious intent, then the cluster admins can safely provide RAM disk to user.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy following deployment with that `replicas` has double number of nodes:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  labels:
    app: memvol
  name: memvol
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: memvol
  strategy: {}
  template:
    metadata:
      creationTimestamp: null
      labels:
        app: memvol
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: busybox
        name: busybox
        command: ["sh"]
        args:
        - "-c"
        - "sleep 5 && dd if=/dev/zero of=/memvol/dump bs=1M count=4000"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: memvol
          mountPath: /memvol
      volumes:
      - name: memvol
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory
```

### Anything else we need to know?

**The point would be how k8s manages memory usage especially in such case of overcommitted memory .
In such cases, the kube-reserved and system-reserved settings are not so effective.**

**Current workaround and its problems**
* Limiting user namespace memory usage using ResourceQuota seems to meet the requirements of a cluster admin. However, I think it would be difficult to get users to accept this, as it would require them to add memory usage information to all manifests.
* I understand that this can be achieved by adding an admission webhook on your own, but I think it would be better if K8s supported it.

title: Update reflector.go to be able to recover from any ResourceVersion
body:
### What happened?

If a controller issues a list request with a large RV, it will not be able to recover from it.
it will get a 500 error as below and relist with the large RV again and again.

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/123823273/50578174-be08-44b1-9eab-622679b2cc64)



the reason is in reflector.go, we only treat expired error and too large resource version error as 'valid' errors and do a relist with RV=0.

```
if isExpiredError(err) || isTooLargeResourceVersionError(err) {
	r.setIsLastSyncResourceVersionUnavailable(true)
	// Retry immediately if the resource version used to list is unavailable.
	// The pager already falls back to full list if paginated list calls fail due to an "Expired" error on
	// continuation pages, but the pager might not be enabled, the full list might fail because the
	// resource version it is listing at is expired or the cache may not yet be synced to the provided
	// resource version. So we need to fallback to resourceVersion="" in all to recover and ensure
	// the reflector makes forward progress.
	list, paginatedResult, err = pager.ListWithAlloc(context.Background(), metav1.ListOptions{ResourceVersion: r.relistResourceVersion()})
}
```
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d4fde1e92a83cb533ae63b3abe9d49f08efb7a2f/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L514



### What did you expect to happen?

we expect controller can recover from http error code 500 and do a relist with RV=0.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. start a latest K8s cluster.
2. update your controller's code starting to list with a large RV that exceeds the range of integer.
3. and you'll be able to see logs like below, the controller will stuck at re-listing.

title: NCC-E003660-HFV: Inaccurate X-Forwarded-Uri Header
body:
### NCC-E003660-HFV: Inaccurate X-Forwarded-Uri Header
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
Systems which receive proxied requests from the API server could receive inaccurate
information about the original URL, and potentially make erroneous security decisions
based on this.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API server’s proxy functionality, implemented in the Transport.RoundTrip
method, adds an `X-Forwarded-Uri` header to the proxied request to indicate the URL of
the original request that was received. The `X-Forwarded-Uri` is constructed by normalizing
the incoming URL, using golang’s `path.Join` method. This will perform processing on the
URL which notably includes resolution of directory traversal sequences ( `../` ) and hence
may produce output which is not an accurate representation of the incoming URL. It should
be noted that the API server does not perform any normalization of the URL before
authorizing, routing, or processing incoming requests. It is possible (although perhaps not
likely) that those systems to which requests are proxied may trust that the `X-Forwarded-
Uri` header is an accurate representation of the URL that was authorized by the API server
when this may not actually be the case.

**Recommendation**
Modify the API server’s proxy functionality so that the `X-Forwarded-Uri` header is an
accurate representation of the original URL.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Location**
Function `RoundTrip()` in file [transport.go:L84](https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/release-1.24/pkg/util/proxy/transport.go#L84)

**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.
The vendor gave this issue an ID of NCC-E003660-HFV and it was finding 12 of the report under the kube-apiserver section.
The vendor considers this issue Low Risk, Low Impact, Low Exploitability
To view the original finding, begin on page 35 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Test Environment**
Kubernetes 1.24.3

title: NCC-E003660-WVM: Logging of Incorrect Bootstrap Tokens
body:
### NCC-E003660-WVM: Logging of Incorrect Bootstrap Tokens
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
Invalid or incorrect bootstrap tokens could be written to the Kubernetes API server logs,
where they may be accessible to attackers or malicious users.

**Description**
When authenticating incoming requests that use bootstrap tokens, the Kubernetes API
server may write secret token values to the log. In this case, token secrets are logged only
if authentication was unsuccessful, which is likely to mean that the secret is not valid.
However, it is possible that the secret is correct apart from a minor error (e.g. a typo) or is a
secret valid elsewhere.

**Recommendation**
Modify this logging statement so that the incorrect token secret value is not included in the
output.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Location**
File [bootstrap.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.24.0/plugin/pkg/auth/authenticator/token/bootstrap/bootstrap.go)

title: NCC-E003660-YVU: Incorrect Handling of Proxy Authentication Headers
body:
### NCC-E003660-YVU: Incorrect Handling of Proxy Authentication Headers
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
If custom values have been set for the authentication proxy header names, an attacker can
assert arbitrary group memberships to extension API servers, leading to privilege
escalation opportunities.

**Description**
The proxy authentication scheme supported by the Kubernetes API server adds custom
HTTP headers to proxied requests to specify username, groups and extra values. These
header names default to `X-Remote-User`, `X-Remote-Group` and `X-Remote-Extra-xxxx`, but
can be changed using command line arguments. The implementation of proxy authentication used by the aggregation layer strips these headers out of incoming requests (to avoid the obvious header spoofing attack), but this code does not take account of the fact that the header names are configurable - instead, it assumes the default values. This means that if the header names _have_ been changed, it will be possible for an attacker to add these headers to a request sent to the Kubernetes API server, and when it is proxied onwards (e.g. to an extension API server) they will not be stripped. The extension API server (assuming that it has been configured with the same header names, as would be expected) would then make security decisions based on these spoofed values: if following the guidance in the Kubernetes documentation, it would include the spoofed information in the `SubjectAccessReview` sent back to the main API server.

It may be the case that a spoofed username header would not be recognized by the destination server, as it is intended that only one of these headers should be present, and the legitimate header added by the aggregation layer may take precedence. However, by design there can be multiple remote group headers so spoofed values would be accepted (and this provides an obvious route for privilege escalation, by adding a group membership
like `system:masters`).

Note that a prerequisite for this attack is to have permission to call the relevant paths on
the extension API server - this will be verified by the main API server before the request is
proxied onwards. The privilege escalation opportunity arises from spoofing the group
memberships which are presented to the extension API server.

**Recommendation**
Modify the SetAuthProxyHeaders method so that it also strips headers with the names
configurable using the `--requestheader-username-headers`, `--requestheader-groupheaders`
and `--requestheader-extra-headers-prefix` options.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Location**
Function `SetAuthProxyHeaders()` in file [round_trippers.go:L124](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.24.0/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/round_trippers.go#L124)

**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.
The vendor gave this issue an ID of NCC-E003660-YVU and it was finding 14 of the report under the kube-apiserver section.
The vendor considers this issue Low Risk, Medium Impact, Low Exploitability
To view the original finding, begin on page 39 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

Kubernetes 1.24.3

title: NCC-E003660-TTV: Timing Side Channel in Bootstrap Tokens Generation and Handling
body:
### NCC-E003660-TTV: Timing Side Channel in Bootstrap Tokens Generation and Handling
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
Attackers may determine Bootstrap Token values based on timing-based side channels.
This may in turn allow them to establish further attacks against a Kubernetes cluster,
including joining nodes to an existing cluster. Feasibility of this attack is contingent on a
number of factors including but not limited to the underlying hardware platform running the
Kubernetes system, and the deployment landscape.

**Description**
Kubernetes Bootstrap Tokens are bearer token credentials employed to authenticate
requests against the API server, when creating new clusters or joining new nodes to an
existing cluster. NCC Group identified a number of functions that handle the Bootstrap
Token, and whose implementations are not constant-time.

The function `randBytes()`, in package `util`, generates Bootstrap Token secret values; it
does so by sampling alphanumeric characters from a table, based on a random secret
index. The access time of a table element, and resulting cache memory contents, may vary
with the access index, which may assist attackers with inferring partial or full information
about a token value.

**Recommendation**
When generating a secret token value, ensure that the selection process from the
alphanumeric table is done in constant-time. The problem is akin to base64 encoding and
decoding in constant-time, as implemented by the BearSSL TLS library.
Given a byte `x` in the 0..35 range, which we want to map to a digit range (ASCII values 48
to 57) and lower case character range (ASCII values 97 to 122), the constant-time selection
process can be achieved as follows: `x + 48 + (39 & ((9 - x) >> 8))`.

In order to increase the level of assurance that the modulo operation is performed in
constant-time on various platforms, and despite changes to compilers, consider modeling
the modulo operation as an explicit multiply and shift operation. The 1991 [Granlund-
Montgomery paper](https://gmplib.org/~tege/divcnst-pldi94.pdf) explains this technique.

Avoid performing regular expression operations on secret data. Consider performing
constant-time comparison of values instead.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Location**
- Function `randBytes()` in file [helpers.go:L84](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8b0e14aeb292deef0c652cd9aab4aaf6da7468/staging/src/k8s.io/cluster-bootstrap/token/util/helpers.go#L84)
- Function `IsValidBootstrapToken()` in file [helpers.go:L97](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8b0e14aeb292deef0c652cd9aab4aaf6da7468/staging/src/k8s.io/cluster-bootstrap/token/util/helpers.go#L97)

title: NCC-E003660-PCK: Non Constant-Time Comparison of Service Account Token Secrets
body:
### NCC-E003660-PCK: Non Constant-Time Comparison of Service Account Token Secrets
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
An attacker may be able to guess a service account token secret, and impersonate the
affected account to read, modify, or delete application data to which the account has
access in a Kubernetes cluster.

**Description**
Service account token secrets (`kubernetes.io/service-account-token`) are a type of
secret used to authenticate service accounts. The “Service account token Secrets” section
of the Kubernetes “Configuration” documentation does not recommend their usage:

> Since 1.22, this type of Secret is no longer used to mount credentials into Pods, and obtaining tokens via the TokenRequest API is recommended instead of using service account token Secret objects. Tokens obtained from the TokenRequest API are more secure than ones stored in Secret objects, because they have a bounded lifetime and are not readable by other API clients. You can use the `kubectl create token` command to obtain a token from the TokenRequest API.

> You should only create a service account token Secret object if you can’t use the TokenRequest API to obtain a token, and the security exposure of persisting a non-expiring token credential in a readable API object is acceptable to you.

Nevertheless, their usage appears to be possible, and may be employed by Kubernetes
users. The process of creating a service account token is documented in the [“Configure
Service Accounts for Pods” documentation section](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/).

An incoming service account request is authenticated by first verifying the JWT signature
of the token, then by comparing the secret token value embedded in the request, against
the server’s record of the value. If the values don’t match, the authentication request is
rejected. The comparison is performed in a non constant-time way; that is, it will return as
soon as it reaches mismatched bytes between the two values. This leaks information about
the token, which may assist attackers in successfully guessing the secret value. The issue
is present in function `Validate()` of file Legacy.go(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8b0e14aeb292deef0c652cd9aab4aaf6da7468/pkg/serviceaccount/legacy.go#L110).

**Recommendation**
Compare the token secret values in constant-time. This can be achieved by using Go’s
[`ConstantTimeCompare()` function](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/subtle#ConstantTimeCompare) of the subtle package.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Location**
Function `Validate()` in file [Legacy.go:L110](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8b0e14aeb292deef0c652cd9aab4aaf6da7468/pkg/serviceaccount/legacy.go#L110)


**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.

title: NCC-E003660-WV3: Privilege Escalation via `nodes/proxy` Permission
body:
### NCC-E003660-WV3: Privilege Escalation via `nodes/proxy` Permission
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
A user with permissions on the `nodes/proxy` subresource in a cluster has full permissions
against the kubelet API on any node by proxying requests through the API server, and can
execute commands in any pod. This may represent privileges beyond those expected by
the cluster administrator, and this situation is not explained in the Kubernetes
documentation.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API server proxy is a feature which allows users to proxy requests through
the API server to workloads or nodes. When a proxy request is made to the kubelet service
on a node, the API server’s own client certificate (which in a typical cluster is a user in the
`system:masters` group) is used to authenticate the request. This effectively allows a user with `get` permissions against the `nodes/proxy` subresource to make `GET` requests to the kubelet
API as `system:masters` (and equivalent for `create`, `patch`, etc.). It is not clear from the
Kubernetes documentation that giving a user permission to make proxied requests to nodes is effectively permitting them to run arbitrary commands against any pod (as can be achieved using the Kubelet API’s `/exec` endpoint).

**Recommendation**
Ensure that the Kubernetes documentation makes it clear that permissions on the `nodes/
proxy` subresource are powerful, overriding other permissions against nodes (as shown
above) and permitting commands to be run in pods.

**Component**
kubelet


**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.

title: [kubelet-image-gc] minimum-image-ttl-duration not work,when kubelet restart.
body:
### What happened?

when kubelet restart,all images which notused cleaned.
but there is a flag in kubelet,`minimum-image-ttl-duration`,explain：Minimum age for an unused image before it is garbage collected.  Examples: '300ms', '10s' or '2h45m'.
i set `minimum-image-ttl-duration` to `20m0s`,it's means if a image not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet（if has disk pressure）.if kubelet not restart, it work,but if restart ther is a bug, `minimum-image-ttl-duration` not work,image will be clean，even if it's no enough  time.


### What did you expect to happen?

`minimum-image-ttl-duration` work, image even if not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1）make node trigger disk pressure.
2）pull some image which not used by pod
3）restart kubelet
4）image cleaned by kubelet after around 10s

### Anything else we need to know?

i see the source code, and maybe there is a bug.

in [detectImages](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L261-L262) func,well detect image and update firstdetect time for every image.
```go
	// New image, set it as detected now.
		if _, ok := im.imageRecords[image.ID]; !ok {
			klog.V(5).InfoS("Image ID is new", "imageID", image.ID)
			im.imageRecords[image.ID] = &imageRecord{
				firstDetected: detectTime,
			}
		}
```
and in  [freeSpace](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L394C1-L397) func,well check images livetime by firstDetected.
```go
		if freeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge {
			klog.V(5).InfoS("Image ID's age is less than the policy's minAge, not eligible for garbage collection", "imageID", image.id, "age", freeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected), "minAge", im.policy.MinAge)
			continue
		}
```
if kubelet running normal,it work,because there is a [Start](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L190-L204) func.
```go
func (im *realImageGCManager) Start() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	go wait.Until(func() {
		// Initial detection make detected time "unknown" in the past.
		var ts time.Time
		if im.initialized {
			ts = time.Now()
		}
                // in first time,ts is zero. 
               // in first time,ts is zero.
		_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)
		if err != nil {
			klog.InfoS("Failed to monitor images", "err", err)
		} else {
			im.initialized = true
		}
	}, 5*time.Minute, wait.NeverStop)
//...

```
in this line,`_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)`,in first time,ts is zero. so image's firstDetected time is zero,and in freeSpace
`reeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge` this check is always false,so image will be cleaned.


maybe we can change to `im.detectImages(time.now())`,can fix this bug.

title: Can't restrict access from K8s nodes with loadBalancerSourceRanges for proxy-mode=ipvs
body:
### What happened?

When using loadBalancerSourceRanges to allow access only from CIDRs outside the cluster segment, access from the K8s nodes (or pods with hostNetwork:true) should be rejected, but for proxy-mode=ipvs it works.

/sig network
/area kube-proxy
/area ipvs

### What did you expect to happen?

Access from K8s nodes should be rejected in the same way as for proxy-mode=iptables

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a service with loadBalancerSourceRanges that allows access from a cidr outside the cluster, e.g.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine
spec:
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
#  - "192.168.1.0/24"
  - "192.168.2.0/24"
#  - "fd00::c0a8:100/120"
  - "fd00::c0a8:200/120"
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  selector:
    app: alpine
  type: LoadBalancer
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  ports:
  - port: 5001
    name: nc
```
The K8s nodes have addresses on 192.168.1.0/24 and fd00::c0a8:100/120.

Make sure a loadBalancerIP is assigned (in this example 10.0.0.0/32) and try to access it from a K8s node:
```
# With proxy.mode=ipvs
> nc 10.0.0.0:5001
alpine-f6c8bd7db-zljnl    # (works)
# With proxy.mode=iptables
# nc 10.0.0.0:5001
# (hangs...)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Same for both ipv4 and ipv6.

This is related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119524 since a fix requires that the `nodeID` passed to the `kube-proxy` is correct. Please see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119524#issuecomment-1655389139

title: Node lease leak caused by lease controller swallowing error
body:
### What happened?

Hello,

We have a cluster that's showing a constant increase in node lease objects. One particularity of the leaked leases is that  they don't have an OwnerReference.

Looking at the code, the ownerReference is set by this kubelet function [`SetNodeOwnerFunc`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/pkg/kubelet/util/nodelease.go#L32) which is called by the lease controller in [`newLease`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go#L230-L233). 

Note that  `newLease` returns `lease` even if the call to `newLeasePostProcessFunc` fails. The means `lease` is returned despite being potentially without an ownerRef.

Looking at `newLease()` call site in [`retryUpdateLease`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go#L187) we see that the returned error is swallowed meaning the controller will make calls to `c.leaseClient.Update` with an incomplete lease.

We don't have access to the worker nodes or the kubelet logs but this explanation match what we are seeing when looking at the audit logs where the call which creates the lease without ownerRef is an Update call.


### What did you expect to happen?

Node lease should always be created with an ownerRef

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To repro, setup a cluster with a worker node, delete the worker node object (but keep the node+kubelet running):
```
kubectl delete no ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal
```
Then look at the lease, the original one will be removed by the GC but kubelet will eventually re-create it without an ownerRef:
```
$ kubectl -n kube-node-lease get lease ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal -o json
{

        "leaseDurationSeconds": 40,
        "renewTime": "2023-07-28T21:06:27.474137Z"
    }
}
```

title: Namespace stuck in Terminating when deleted if ApiService doesn't implement Aggregated Discovery
body:
### What happened?

We implement a manual `APIService` API Extension in [Agones](https://github.com/googleforgames/agones).

Definition:
https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/blob/main/install/helm/agones/templates/service/allocation.yaml

Code for handling web requests:
https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/blob/main/pkg/util/apiserver/apiserver.go

The code is extremely lightweight as we only have no need for storage, and only accept CREATE requests at this time.

This issue was first reported by one of our users in May, but we only were able to reproduce it ourselves once we were on 1.27.x: https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/issues/3172

Testing on Kubernetes 1.27.x we noticed that when attempting to delete Namespaces, they would get stuck in termination with the following description:

```
❯ kubectl describe ns 1690585578
Name:         1690585578
Labels:       kubernetes.io/metadata.name=1690585578
              owner=e2e-test
Annotations:  <none>
Status:       Terminating
Conditions:
  Type                                         Status  LastTransitionTime               Reason                  Message
  ----                                         ------  ------------------               ------                  -------
  NamespaceDeletionDiscoveryFailure            True    Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:07:44 -0700  DiscoveryFailed         Discovery failed for some groups, 1 failing: unable to retrieve the complete list of server APIs: allocation.agones.dev/v1: stale GroupVersion discovery: allocation.agones.dev/v1
  NamespaceDeletionGroupVersionParsingFailure  False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:07:46 -0700  ParsedGroupVersions     All legacy kube types successfully parsed
  NamespaceDeletionContentFailure              False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:08:56 -0700  ContentDeleted          All content successfully deleted, may be waiting on finalization
  NamespaceContentRemaining                    False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:08:56 -0700  ContentRemoved          All content successfully removed
  NamespaceFinalizersRemaining                 False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:08:56 -0700  ContentHasNoFinalizers  All content-preserving finalizers finished
```

So far, I've not found a way to delete the Namespace.

Looking through the log for the webserver, i can see requests for `/apis` and the new Aggregated Discovery feature (`Accept:  "application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList"`), but we return a 404 to that response, since it's not implemented.

Looking through the code I can find (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.27.3/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go) it seems that any response other than `http.StatusOK` would result in this issue -- which is breaking backward compatibility within `APIService` to assume that this API surface is implemented in some way.


### What did you expect to happen?

Namespaces would terminate as per normal.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install Agones on a cluster (https://agones.dev/site/docs/installation/install-agones/)
2. `kubectl create ns foo`
3. `kubectl delete ns foo`
4. Watch as the ns gets stuck in Terminating.



### Anything else we need to know?

If I had a magic wand, I'd love a reference of all the API's that get called against an APIService and what their expected results should be.

So far it's a combo of using `kubectl proxy` and looking at the k8s API responses, crawling through code, and reading apiserver logs to try and reverse engineer this work.

title: /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus Not Found In Privileged Pod from Kubernetes 1.24 onwards with Cgroups V2
body:
### What happened?

In Kubernetes version 1.24 and onwards (Testing on K8s 1.23 does not show the error), I am seeing an issue whereby the file `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus` (used by my application to read what CPUs have been assigned to the container by the K8s CPU Manager) disappears when the container is privileged. With a non-privileged container, the file `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus` is accessible. This error is occuring with Cgroups V2 (I have not tested with Cgroups V1). It looks to me that in newer versions of Kubernetes (1.24 and onwards) the host directory  `/sys/fs/cgroup/` is being mounted into privileged containers thus overwriting the containers own Cgroup fs. If this is expected, it would be good to know what way an application in a privileged container should retrieve it's assigned CPUs now that it no longer has access to it's own individual `/sys/fs/cgroup/` directory.

### What did you expect to happen?

In a K8s privileged container, I would expect it should have access to its own individual `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On the following setup, perform the proceeding steps:
**Kubernetes Version:** 1.26.2 (Note this can be replicated on 1.24 and onwards)
**Cgroup driver:** systemd
**Containerd Version:** 1.6.20
**OS Version:** Ubuntu 22.04.2
**Kernel:** 5.15.0-76-generic

Start off with a very simple pod spec (`test.yaml`):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-0
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: "node1"
  containers:
    - name: pod-0
      image: ubuntu:22.04
      command: [ "/bin/sh" , "-c", "tail -f /dev/null" ]
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 4
          memory: 2Gi
        limits:
          cpu: 4
          memory: 2Gi
```
Start the pod and exec into it:
```bash
kubectl apply -f test.yaml 
kubectl exec -it test-0 -- /bin/bash
```
Once in the container, run the following:
```bash
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus
```
The output is similar to: `44,46,100,102` (i.e the cpus allocated to my pod are printed as expected using cgroupv2 filesystem)

Next I remove the pod (`kubectl delete pod test-0`) and create a new pod with the following spec (Note the new privileged securityContext):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-0
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: "node1"
  containers:
    - name: pod-0
      image: ubuntu:22.04
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
        privileged: true
      command: [ "/bin/sh" , "-c", "tail -f /dev/null" ]
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 4
          memory: 2Gi
        limits:
          cpu: 4
          memory: 2Gi
```
Same as before, I start the pod and exec into it:
```bash
kubectl apply -f test.yaml 
kubectl exec -it test-0 -- /bin/bash
```
Again, once in the container, I run the following:
```bash
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus
```
But this time I get the following error:
```
cat: /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus: No such file or directory
```
Thus this shows that adding privileged mode to the container removes the container cgroupv2 entry `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset.cpus`

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Our Developers are developing springboot java application and which are deploying to AKS cluster. We have Helm and Azure pipelines to deploy these apps to the AKS cluster dynamically and the values for the Pod resource speicification are defined in Variablegroups of the ADO pipelines and.

 But we are facing some difficlties to estimate the required resource specification for their each apps,because each apps has different JVM settings and startup behaviour. Since we dont have a proper mechanisam inplace to define the Resource Request and Limit (Cpu and Mem respectively), our clutsers are over committed by the mis usage of these values in ADO pipelines.

So we are trying to introduce some automated mechanism, where a developer can estimate their required memory& cpu request and limit values by passing their JVM arguments or some specific things to be considered for springboot application, then these estimated values can be used in the corresponding Variables groups. below are the some components which are used in jvmSetings. 

So is this possible to achieve in an automated way ? 

Below are the some of the jvmSettings parameters used by the developers

```
-Xmx650m 
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100
-XX:MetaspaceSize=150m
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=150m 
-XX:MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio=100
-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize=25m
-XX:InitialCodeCacheSize=100m
-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=100m
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=100m
-XX:+DisableExplicitGC
```


### Why is this needed?

This is needed to define the actual resource specifications than over committing any unused resource

title: why my podstat.ContainerStats.Logs.UsedBytes continued rise?
Pod created without UID cannot be removed
body:
### What happened?

When a new pod is created through the CRI API (using `crictl`), it is able to be created without a UID. When removing the pod, an error occurs: 
```
getting sandbox status of pod "ec38fa6b815da5cd3ab2ac168dc8ec9133bced169d8a8790280ea7cd24ea0470": metadata.Name, metadata.Namespace or metadata.Uid is not in metadata "&PodSandboxMetadata{Name:wwcritestpod,Uid:,Namespace:wwcritest,Attempt:0,}"
```
This leaves no way to remove pods that have been created without a UID.
The above error is generated from this function: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/56f6030125d737dd031d77f45af6a413d1990862/pkg/kubelet/cri/remote/remote_runtime.go#L272

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should be successfully removed. Or a pod without a UID in the pod configuration should not be allowed to be created.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use `crictl` to create a pod without a UID:

1. Create the container and sandbox configuration files (see below)
2. `crictl runp sandbox-config.json`
3. `crictl create <pod-id> container-config.json sandbox-config.json`
4. `crictl start <container-id>`
5. `crictl stop <container-id>`
6. `crictl rm <container-id>`
7. `crictl stopp <pod-id>`
8. `crictl rmp <pod-id>` results in the described error, unable to remove the pod sandbox.

sandbox-config.json:
```
{
        "metadata": {
                "name": "nginx-sandbox",
                "namespace": "default",
                "attempt": 1
        },
        "linux": {}
}
```

container-config.json:
```
{
  "metadata": {
      "name": "busybox"
  },
  "image":{
      "image": "busybox"
  },
  "command": [
      "top"
  ],
  "linux": {
  }
}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

It is unclear whether the UID value is required at the time of pod creation, as it does not currently create an error when starting a new pod with no UID. It is also unclear if the responsibility of enforcing the UID, if required, falls onto the client or the underlying runtime (containerd, CRI-O, etc.).

title: Trace exemplars for kube-apiserver metrics
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add exemplars to APIServer metrics.  To accomplish this, we need to add FooWithExemplar functions, like histograms ObserveWithExemplar to component-base/metrics: 
https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/blob/7f2db5f1ed43d8a4312bfd85280a17dfef13358b/prometheus/histogram.go#L722 At minimum, we should allow exemplars on counters and histograms.

Then, we need to change Observe() calls to ObserveWithExemplar calls, similar to https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/blob/main/examples/exemplars/main.go.

We should use the `trace_id` key for the trace ID, and the `span_id` key for the span ID.

cc @Richabanker @kubernetes/sig-instrumentation-leads 


### Why is this needed?

With https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/647, we can now collect traces for requests to the kubernetes api.  We have a number of metrics, such as `apiserver_request_duration_seconds`, which would benefit from having exemplars attached.

title: Service `status.loadBalancer.ingress` can be set when `type` != `LoadBalancer`
body:
xref 119454

I think this may be one of the few cases where we can actually change the behavior in a "breaking" way.

User creates service with `.type=ClusterIP`, `.status.loadBalancer` is empty
Controller or user updates the status subresource, sets `.spec.loadBalancer.ingress[].ip` (not wiped or validated, should be)
User updates `service spec` in any way, `.staus.loadBalancer` is wiped

It's clear that the `.status.loadBalancer` is not meant to be set when `.type` is not "LoadBalancer".

The question is:

1) Fail validation?
2) Silently discard the value?
3) Warn and then discard the value?
4) Just warn and leave it.

Because we allowed it in the past, but it is so volatile, I lean towards 3.

@aojea and @khenidak - the people most familair with this type.

Edit: PrepareForUpdate() runs before warnings.  So:

(1) is easy
(2) is easy
(4) is slightly less easy than (2)
(3) is slightly less easy than (4)

title: minimum-image-ttl-duration is not working after restart kubelet
body:
### What happened?

When a node is under disk pressure, restarting kubelet will lead to image gc immediately, even if we set a long `minimum-image-ttl-duration`.

### What did you expect to happen?

image gc honor `minimum-image-ttl-duration` when we restart kubelet of a node under disk pressure.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. configuring a long `minimum-image-ttl-duration`, e.g. 10m.  (`minimum-image-ttl-duration`'s default value is 2 minutes, which is short enough to make many people overlook this issue.)
2. make sure node is under disk pressure, e.g. nodefs utilization 85%+ (without imagefs)
3. pull new image on disk pressure node, make sure there are unused images on this node
4. restart kubelet
5. after a short time, all unused images will be gc, and `minimum-image-ttl-duration` is not yet reached

title: Adapt swap jobs to run with cgroup v2
body:
**Context**:
NodeSwap feature gate was recently [graduated to Beta1](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4128). Currently, as per [the KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2400-node-swap), swap is only supported with cgroup v2 - cgroup v1 is no longer supported.

For this reason, we decided to fail kubelet if NodeSwap feature gate is enabled and the node runs with cgroup v1. This would help prevent any surprises for the user by failing as soon as possible. This effort is being implemented in this PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119327.

**The problem**:
Currently, swap jobs are running with cgroup v1. Swap tests were added in a way that they first check on which environment they're being run (e.g. which cgroup version? is NodeSwap FG enabled? Which swapBehavior is defined? etc) and then expect the right behavior to take place. With v1, the tests expect the containers to be defined without swap access.

While the tests pass, they are much less valuable, since all they check is that swap is disabled for v1 workloads. The tests would be much more valuable if they would run with v2, therefore actually ensure that proper swap limitations are configured.

In addition, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119327 is dependent on these changes, since as of now the jobs immediately fail with this PR since kubelet fails on an environment with cgroup v1 and swap enabled.

**What needs to change**:
- [x] CRI-O swap related jobs should be defined to run with cgroup v2 (e.g. `pull-kubernetes-node-swap-fedora`)
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/30242
- [x] containerd swap related jobs should be defined to run with cgroup v2 (e.g. `pull-kubernetes-node-swap-ubuntu-serial`).
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/30297

**Future work**:
In the future, we might consider introducing more jobs to check swap. Ideally, both `LimitedSwap` and `UnlimitedSwap` would be tested, perhaps by periodic jobs.

title: PodDisruptionBudget with an empty selector `{}` being honored incorrectly
body:
### What happened?

`PodDisruptionBudget` with an empty selector `{}` selects all the pods as expected.
But, during the `drain` /`eviction`, the pdb is not being honored correctly i.e. all the pods are getting evicted.

This issue is only observed with the empty selector and works as expected if a valid label selector is provided that selects all the pods in a namespace.

### What did you expect to happen?

When an empty selector `{}` is provided in the `PodDisruptionBudget`'s spec, the created `PodDisruptionBudget` needs to be honored by not evicting all the pods during the `drain/eviction` api call

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: busybox
  name: busybox
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: busybox
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: busybox
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: busybox
        name: busybox
        command: ["sleep", "1000"]
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

title: CEL Estimated cost incorrect for lowerAscii
body:
### What happened?

Creating a CRD with a case-insensitive uniqueness check and appropriate maxLength/maxItems limits should be allowed:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: uniquetests.stable.example.com
spec:
  group: stable.example.com
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                headers:
                  type: array
                  maxItems: 1
                  x-kubernetes-validations:
                    - rule: "self.all(item1, self.exists_one(item2, item1.name.lowerAscii() == item2.name.lowerAscii()))"
                  items:
                    type: object
                    properties:
                      name:
                        maxLength: 1
                        type: string
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: uniquetests
    singular: uniquetest
    kind: UniqueTest
```

But I got:

```
kubectl apply -f unique.yaml
The CustomResourceDefinition "uniquetests.stable.example.com" is invalid: 
* spec.validation.openAPIV3Schema.properties[spec].properties[headers].x-kubernetes-validations[0].rule: Forbidden: estimated rule cost exceeds budget by factor of more than 100x (try simplifying the rule, or adding maxItems, maxProperties, and maxLength where arrays, maps, and strings are declared)
* spec.validation.openAPIV3Schema.properties[spec].properties[headers].x-kubernetes-validations[0].rule: Forbidden: contributed to estimated rule cost total exceeding cost limit for entire OpenAPIv3 schema
* spec.validation.openAPIV3Schema: Forbidden: x-kubernetes-validations estimated rule cost total for entire OpenAPIv3 schema exceeds budget by factor of more than 100x (try simplifying the rule, or adding maxItems, maxProperties, and maxLength where arrays, maps, and strings are declared)
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the estimated cost to be very low with maxItems=1 and maxLength=1.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This also exceeds the estimated cost limit, suggesting the problem is unrelated to the array:

```yaml
 x-kubernetes-validations:                                                                                        
  - rule: "self[0].name.lowerAscii() == self[0].name.lowerAscii()"
```

But this is valid (estimated cost is under the limit):

```yaml
x-kubernetes-validations:                                                                                        
  - rule: "self.all(item1, self.exists_one(item2, item1.name == item2.name))"
```

Which suggests that the estimated cost system is not handling `lowerAscii` correctly.  The estimated cost of `lowerAscii` should be a function of the input string length (which in this case has a max length of 1), and, for purposes of subsequent cost calculations, the resulting value of `lowerAscii` should be known by the estimated cost system to be the same length as the input string.



### Anything else we need to know?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/cost.go#L119 is where the estimated cost of lowerAscii is handled. Just glancing at the code I don't see an obvious problem.

### Kubernetes version

title: Bind mounting Kubelet root-dir causes staging volumes to never be cleaned up for ReadWriteMany PVCs
body:
### What happened?

For various reasons I have an installation of Kubelet on all nodes in a cluster bind mounted to another location on disk. When a volume is staged on a node this causes the staging volume to appear twice when running the `mount` command. Here's an example of such an instance with a pod on the node,

```
~$ mount | grep pvc-my-volume
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid on /some/path/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount type <scrub>
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid on /var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount type <scrub>
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid on /some/path/kubelet/pods/pod-id/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-my-volume/mount type <scrub>
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid/pod-id on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/pod-id/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-my-volume/mount type <scrub>
```

How ever when the pod is deleted you would expect all of these mounts to be removed since no pods are on the node anymore requiring the volume, and `NodeUnstageVolume` should be called on the CSI.

If you take a look in the logs you'll see an error (only the error is here to scrub info from the log)
`kubelet[6307]: 6307 nestedpendingoperations.go:301] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/<scrub> podName: nodeName:}" failed. Error: "GetDeviceMountRefs check failed for volume \"pvc-my-volume\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/csi/<scrub>\") on node \"my-node\" : the device mount path \"/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount\" is still mounted by other references [/some/path/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount]"`

This is caused by this check
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L947-L955

Which fails on a false flag that the mount is itself the reference. This seems to only happen on `ReadWriteMany` volumes, and we particularly noticed because we're using ceph-csi with CephFS and RBD. We sometimes have clients holding onto locks for folders and files in these staging mounts, and normally you'd delete the pod and the lock would be free, but due to this they stick around and the only fix is to manually umount the path. This doesn't happen for RBD as Kubelet correctly calls `NodeUnstageVolume` for the CSI plugin, but not CephFS.

### What did you expect to happen?

When all pods are removed from a node then Kubelet should call `NodeUnstageVolume` for the given CSI plugin and not error out.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install Rook and setup a Ceph cluster with CephFS
2. Create a PVC with a storage class for CephFS and access mode `ReadWriteMany`
3. On a node bind mount `/var/lib/kubelet` to another directory on disk (IE `bind --mount /var/lib/kubelet /tmp/kubelet`
4. On this same node, schedule a pod and mount the PVC
5. Observe 4 mounts for this pod, 2 staging and 2 regular
6. Delete the pod
7. Observe 2 staging mounts for this PVC and errors in kubelet logs

### Anything else we need to know?

I have already tested a fix for this and located where to fix it.

The issue stems from here 
https://github.com/kubernetes/mount-utils/blob/41e8de37ef8a3782f9cd6c915699b98b2b24b2c4/mount_linux.go#L687-L728

This specific function is just looping through all mounts and checking the root path, and major:minor of the mounts. While this works generally, once you bind mount the `/var/lib/kubelet` directory this will always return 1 reference to all staging mounts.

If you inspect the mountinfo on the node (where this is getting the info), you'll notice that the parent IDs for the `/var/lib/kubelet` mounts are all the same but the bind mounted ones are not.

We can then make this change to fix it
```
+       parentID := 0
        rootPath := ""
        major := -1
        minor := -1
@@ -566,6 +568,7 @@ func SearchMountPoints(hostSource, mountInfoPath string) ([]string, error) {
                if hostSource == mis[i].MountPoint || PathWithinBase(hostSource, mis[i].MountPoint) {
                        // If it's a mount point or path under a mount point.
                        mountID = mis[i].ID
+                       parentID = mis[i].ParentID
                        rootPath = filepath.Join(mis[i].Root, strings.TrimPrefix(hostSource, mis[i].MountPoint))
                        major = mis[i].Major
                        minor = mis[i].Minor
@@ -579,8 +582,8 @@ func SearchMountPoints(hostSource, mountInfoPath string) ([]string, error) {
 
        var refs []string
        for i := range mis {
-               if mis[i].ID == mountID {
-                       // Ignore mount entry for mount source itself.
+               if mis[i].ID == mountID || mis[i].ParentID != parentID {
+                       // Ignore mount entry for mount source itself, and other refs that don't have the same parentID.
                        continue
                }
                if mis[i].Root == rootPath && mis[i].Major == major && mis[i].Minor == minor {
```

I made these changes locally, built Kubelet, and setup my test node with the patched Kubelet and the staging directory was removed and `NodeUnstageVolume` was called in my CSI plugin with no issues.

I do not believe this should affect any other use case as realistically any mount based on the staging mount should have the same Parent ID. I'm happy to make a PR for this if this is found to be an acceptable solution.

title: sched: CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins not always injected into cycleState
body:
### What happened?

In k8s 1.27, scheduler introduced a new "short circuit" semantics in PreFilter to bypass a Pod quickly. A change introduced here is it relies on that plugin to be stored in `CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins`, which makes sense as what it was explained [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114125/files#r1062646736).

However, the `SkipFilterPlugins` info, although is populated upon each plugin's PreFilter invocation, is not injected into `CycleState` when some PreFilter returns unschedulable:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L655-L661

So think about this workflow:

- pluginA returns Skip in its PreFilter
- pluginB return Unschedulable in its PreFilter
- note: pluginA is not included in `CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins` due to aforementioned bug
- a Pod is claimed as unschedulable (failed by pluginB)
- during PostFilter, it's **supposed** to bypass pluginA's PreEnqueueExtension's AddPod/RemovePod, but it doesn't
- calling a "skipped" Plugin's AddPod/RemovePod during preemption, sometimes will abort the whole preemption as the logic tries to read info from cycleState, and some plugin's "skip" version doesn't fill cycleState properly, e.g., InterPodAffinity (skip immediately w/o write preFilterStateKey).

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/interpodaffinity/filtering.go#L257-L262

### What did you expect to happen?

Short circuiting using Skip is fine, but `CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins` should injected properly at all cases.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Described in the workflow above.

It's firstly captured in an out-of-tree PostFilter plugin: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins/pull/608#issuecomment-1665855370, but can also happen in in-tree plugins.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

body:
Move @sanposhiho 's https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119769#pullrequestreview-1563700339 here as a new discussion thread:

Kensei pointed out a potential bug in the scheduling path when we hit Unschedulable result in one of PreFilter plugins:

> - pluginA returns Unschedulable in its PreFilter.
> - (Because pluginA returns unschedulable, RunPreFilterPlugins() is aborted at that point and pluginB PreFIlter isn't executed)
> - a Pod is claimed as unschedulable (failed by pluginA)
> - calling a pluginB's AddPod/RemovePod during preemption, sometimes will abort the whole preemption as the logic tries to read info from cycleState.

title: [It] [sig-network] "Services should create endpoints for unready pods" should not depend on kube-proxy for validation
body:
### What happened?

**[Kubernetes e2e suite: [It] [sig-network] Services should create endpoints for unready pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/test/e2e/network/service.go#L1752-L1835)**

This test validates the existence of endpoints of unready pods of a service (with  PublishNotReadyAddresses: true) by probing service with curl requests, in other words depend on kube-proxy to check if the endpoints exists for the service with unready pods. 


### What did you expect to happen?

If I'm not wrong, the purpose of setting `PublishNotReadyAddresses: true` is to make sure the endpoint/endpointslices exists even if the pods are not ready to make sure coredns is able to create A/AAAA records. 

The test should simply check if the endpoints/endpointslices exists for the given service rather than expecting a response from the curl request, i.e. should not depend on kube-proxy.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/test/e2e/network/service.go#L4195-L4196

There are some discussions https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119394#discussion_r1282269250 going on to ignore **Ready**  condition and only use **Serving** and **Terminating** for programming data path. This test becomes a blocker for that task. 


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The test currently passes as kube-proxy currently uses `EndpointConditions.Ready` for programming endpoints. 
Switching from `EndpointConditions.Ready` -> `EndpointConditions.Serving && !EndpointConditions.Terminating` fails the test. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/staging/src/k8s.io/endpointslice/utils.go#L36-L42

title: CronJob gets stuck when jobs quota is reached
body:
### What happened?

We (in Booking.com) run CronJobs in Kubernetes clusters with ResourceQuota's defined. When quota for # of jobs is reached we observed that CronJobs:
1. stop scheduling new jobs (because quota is reached),
2. don't clean the old jobs (despite # of jobs > history allows and the fact that it would unblock the CronJob new Jobs). 

The only way to progress is to remove enough Jobs to make room for a new Job in namespace quota. When we do that manually, the CronJob kicks in.

The workaround we found around the internet is to specify `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` for the job template. But it's not ideal as it's not a history-based limit, but a time-based limit, and often you want to have the last N jobs to be around for debugging.

### What did you expect to happen?

When jobs quota is reached and # of cronjob jobs exceeds specified the history limit, these jobs are deleted giving room for new jobs to run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: job-quota
  namespace: default
spec:
  hard:
    count/jobs.batch: "1"
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: hello-world-cronjob
spec:
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 0
  schedule: "* * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: hello-world
              image: bash
              command: ["bash", "-c", "sleep 80"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

1. Wait for a first Job to be created (which will fill up the jobs quota) at X minute.
2. A job for X + 1 will fail to be created (because quota won't allow, and X job is still running).
3. All future attempts to create a new job by the controller will fail (check `kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail`, you'll see re-occuring `Error creating job: jobs.batch "hello-world-cronjob-28187648" is forbidden: exceeded quota: job-quota, requested: count/jobs.batch=1, used: count/jobs.batch=1, limited: count/jobs.batch=1`).
4. The first job will never be cleaned (although it will be eligible, since history is 0).

### Anything else we need to know?

Looks like the problem was introduced in the `cronjob_controllerv2.go` implementation: if `jm.syncCronJob` returned an error, we return from the function and never invoke `jm.cleanupFinishedJobs`.:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L199-L213

In the old `cronjob_controller.go` implementation this was not the case:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f77da5bd4809927e15d1658fb4aa8f13ad890a5/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controller.go#L137-L138

body:
When PreFilter returns UnschedulableAndUnresolvable, we don't need to run the preemption, but currently we run.
This unexpected preemption could cause errors from the preemption by trying to read non-exist PreFilter data.

As @Huang-Wei pointed out ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119770#issuecomment-1666418637)), actually we didn't run the preemption in such cases in the past versions, but https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110894 introduced this bug.

/kind bug 
/kind regression
/sig scheduling
/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

title: scheduler: register default EventsToRegister in only some extension points
body:
## What

register default EventsToRegister only for PreFilter, Filter, Reserve, and Permit plugins.

Currently, we register default EventsToRegister for all plugins that don't have EnqueueExtension.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L551-L554

## Why

EventsToRegister affects which events the scheduler watches, and when registered events come, the scheduling queue requeue Pods according to them. The queue checks the event can make Pod schedulable or not via QueueingHint from pInfo.UnschedulablePlugins.
Given this fact, plugins that never be registered in pInfo.UnschedulablePlugins don't need to have EventsToRegister. 
And, currently, only PreFilter, Filter, Reserve, and Permit affect pInfo.UnschedulablePlugins. Meaning all other plugins' EventsToRegister actually don't affect anything, and to register default EventsToRegister to other plugins could result in watching events in vain, which all of PreFilter, Filter, Reserve, and Permit plugins aren't interested in.

/kind feature
/sig scheduling
