### What happened?

Update "kubernetes" endpoint by moving `subsets[0].addresses` to `subsets[0].notReadyAddresses` and the kube-apiserver keep logging
```
...
Resetting endpoints for master service "kubernetes" to [x.x.x.x]
...
"HTTP" verb="GET" URI="/api/v1/namespaces/default/endpoints/kubernetes"
"HTTP" verb="PUT" URI="/api/v1/namespaces/default/endpoints/kubernetes"
...
// The same log is continuously printed.
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The `ReconcileEndpoints` shows that following steps will be performed under the condition mentioned earlier:

1. Currently the "kubernetes" endpoint struct is (We manually updated it):
```
  subsets:
  - notReadyAddresses:
    - ip: x.x.x.x
```
2. Since currently "kube-apiserver" is healthy in fact (we just manually update the endpoint), the "kubernetes" endpoint struct will first be constructed as: 
```
  subsets:
  - addresses:
    - ip: x.x.x.x
```
3. And then `RepackSubsets` is called so the "kubernetes" endpoint struct will be updated to
```
  // the struct has no changes compared to the current "kubernetes" endpoint struct
  subsets:
  - notReadyAddresses:
    - ip: x.x.x.x
```

In such condition, I think either the "kubernetes" endpoint should be updated by moving `subsets[0].notReadyAddresses` back to `subsets[0].addresses`, or not sending an update request

title: Cleanup: Validate pod terminationGracePeriodSeconds and fix tests
body:
xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119026/files#r1265687485

Apparently we do not validate that the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` field is non-nil.  It has a default value, so it should never actually be nil, but because we never validated it in the past, we have tests that do not set it.

We should remove code which check for nil, like the above comment:

```
	var gracePeriod int64
	if spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds != nil {
		// this could happen in tests
		gracePeriod = *spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds
	}
```

This will cause a bunch of tests to fail.  Those tests SHOULD be setting this field properly.  See "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/api/service/testing" which has helper functions for the same problem in Service.

title: APIService's status blocked on FailedDiscoveryCheck condition with 503
body:
### What happened?

We meet a problem that the APISerivce is blocked on the FailedDiscoveryCheck condition:
```
status:
  conditions:
  - lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-15T16:35:28Z"
    message: 'failing or missing response from https://12.4.170.157:6443/apis/cluster.alauda.io/v1:
      bad status from https://12.4.170.157:6443/apis/cluster.alauda.io/v1: 503'
    reason: FailedDiscoveryCheck
    status: "False"
    type: Available
```

But we get the right response by directly accessing the endpoint:
```
# curl -ik https://12.4.170.157:6443/apis/cluster.alauda.io/v1 --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/front-proxy-client.crt --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/front-proxy-client.key -H 'X-Remote-User: system:kube-aggregator' -H 'X-Remote-Group: system:masters'
HTTP/2 200
audit-id: 63a060ef-1e42-4fc0-8d00-d859cddd0763
cache-control: no-cache, private
content-type: application/json
content-length: 393
date: Mon, 16 Oct 2023 02:34:19 GMT

{
  "kind": "APIResourceList",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "groupVersion": "cluster.alauda.io/v1",
  "resources": [
    {
      "name": "clusterviews",
      "singularName": "",
      "namespaced": true,
      "kind": "ClusterView",
      "verbs": [
        "delete",
        "deletecollection",
        "get",
        "list",
        "patch",
        "update",
        "watch"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

We also checked the endpoints and the IPVS rules, and all of them looked well.

We have met this problem several times. Rebuilding the pods can not make the APIService become ready.
The only way we found that can resolve it temporally is to restart the kube-apiserver.




### What did you expect to happen?

The APIService works well.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It's hard to reproduce it. After reading the source code, we think reproducing the problem needs these conditions:
1. The endpoint of the APIService uses the 6443 port which is also the kube-apiserver's port.
2. The Service existed before but is without the APIService's port, Update the Service to add APIService's port and Create the APIService at almost the same time.
3. The kube-apiservice checks the APISerivice's endpoint when the service IP has been bound to the `kube-ipvs0` network card, but the IPVS rule has not been generated.

The following example may reproduce it:
`kubectl create -f  demo-apiservice-1.yaml`

```
# demo-apiservice-1.yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: demo-apiservice
  namespace: default
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: demo-apiservice
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  annotations:
  generation: 1
  labels:
    app: demo-apiservice
  name: demo-apiservice
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo-apiservice
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo-apiservice
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx:alpine
        name: demo-apiservice
```
Wait several seconds to let the Service and Deployment work.

Then 
`kubectl apply -f demo-apiservice-2.yaml`

```
# demo-apiservice-1.yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: demo-apiservice
  namespace: default
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
    name: port-80
  - port: 6443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
    name: port-6443
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: demo-apiservice
---
apiVersion: apiregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: APIService
metadata:
  name: v1.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  groupPriorityMinimum: 1000
  insecureSkipTLSVerify: true
  service:
    name: demo-apiservice
    namespace: default
    port: 6443
  version: v1
  versionPriority: 1
```

Then look at the APIService's status.
` kubectl get apiservice v1.example.com -o yaml`

You may see:
```
apiVersion: apiregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: APIService
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"apiregistration.k8s.io/v1","kind":"APIService","metadata":{"annotations":{},"name":"v1.example.com"},"spec":{"group":"example.com","groupPriorityMinimum":1000,"insecureSkipTLSVerify":true,"service":{"name":"demo-apiservice","namespace":"default","port":6443},"version":"v1","versionPriority":1}}
  creationTimestamp: "2023-10-16T03:41:33Z"
  name: v1.example.com
  resourceVersion: "721774"
  uid: 47c46244-1dc4-4af0-932a-dc78f2c47585
spec:
  group: example.com
  groupPriorityMinimum: 1000
  insecureSkipTLSVerify: true
  service:
    name: demo-apiservice
    namespace: default
    port: 6443
  version: v1
  versionPriority: 1
status:
  conditions:
  - lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-16T03:41:33Z"
    message: 'failing or missing response from https://172.108.103.208:6443/apis/example.com/v1:
      bad status from https://172.108.103.208:6443/apis/example.com/v1: 503'
    reason: FailedDiscoveryCheck
    status: "False"
    type: Available
```






### Anything else we need to know?

By digging into the source code we found these implementations work together may cause this problem.

1. The APIService's `AvailableConditionController` uses a cached transport by `transport.New(transportConfig)` which uses `rt, err = tlsCache.get(config)` to get a cached transport. This causes the HTTP clients to always use the same socket to access the APISerivce's service IP.
2. We use kube-proxy's  IPVS mod. The Service existed before but is without the APIService's port. So there is the Service's IP on the `kube-ipvs0` dummy network card. But there isn't the APISerivce's Port in the IPVS entries until the Service has been updated.  If we access the Service IP with the APIServer's port now, we actually access the endpoint on the host. Unfortunately, there is the same port 6443 on the host that can answer this access.
3. After the kube-apiserver has built the socket to the 6443 port with Service IP (actually accessing the 6443 port on the host), the cached transport lets it keep using the same socket. And the IPVS won't break the existing socket even if the rules have been updated.

So all of the above worked together caused my problem. We are planning to change to another port for the APIService to avoid this kind of wrong access.

title: [code-generator] Breaking `gen_client()` function in `kube_codegen` script
body:
### What would you like to be added?

`gen_client()` function in `kube_codegen` script has following issues:
- `gen_client()` function only supports `types.go` file  https://github.com/kubernetes/code-generator/blob/e4611069dfb4b0c04c7751afae1b9fef64828964/kube_codegen.sh#L539-L544 but we have multiple types file with name as `type_*.go` in [our repo](https://github.com/gardener/gardener/tree/master/pkg/apis/core). Hence this function is not working in our case.
For the mitigation there is already an open [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119981). I have asked for including our changes as well.
- We have multiple types_*.go files under a [pkg](https://github.com/gardener/gardener/tree/master/pkg/apis/seedmanagement) for example `types_managedseed.go` and `types_managedseedset.go`. Because of this `--input-dirs github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/apis/seedmanagement/v1alpha1` for `informer-gen` appears twice and it generates duplicate informers
```
// Group=seedmanagement.gardener.cloud, Version=v1alpha1
case v1alpha1.SchemeGroupVersion.WithResource("managedseeds"):
	return &genericInformer{resource: resource.GroupResource(), informer: f.Seedmanagement().V1alpha1().ManagedSeeds().Informer()}, nil
case v1alpha1.SchemeGroupVersion.WithResource("managedseeds"):
	return &genericInformer{resource: resource.GroupResource(), informer: f.Seedmanagement().V1alpha1().ManagedSeeds().Informer()}, nil
case v1alpha1.SchemeGroupVersion.WithResource("managedseedsets"):
	return &genericInformer{resource: resource.GroupResource(), informer: f.Seedmanagement().V1alpha1().ManagedSeedSets().Informer()}, nil
case v1alpha1.SchemeGroupVersion.WithResource("managedseedsets"):
	return &genericInformer{resource: resource.GroupResource(), informer: f.Seedmanagement().V1alpha1().ManagedSeedSets().Informer()}, nil
```
We only need unique elements before passing it to `informer-gen`. I followed this approach for unique elements:
```bash
input_pkgs=($(echo "${input_pkgs1[@]}" | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' '))
group_versions=($(echo "${group_versions1[@]}" | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' '))
```
- We have packages under `pkg/apis/<package_name>` [refer](https://github.com/gardener/gardener/tree/master/pkg/apis) . Earlier we were generating client only for `pkg/apis/core` and `pkg/apis/seedmanagement`. But with the new `kube-codegen` I am not able to do that.
I am using the following call to `gen_client` function:
```
kube::codegen::gen_client \
    --with-watch \
    --input-pkg-root github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/apis/seedmanagement \
    --output-pkg-root github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/client/seedmanagement \
    --output-base "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../.." \
    --boilerplate "${PROJECT_ROOT}/hack/LICENSE_BOILERPLATE.txt"
```
It results in following flags to `client-gen`
```
--input-base : github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/apis/seedmanagement
--output-base : github.com/gardener/gardener/hack/../../../..
--output-package : github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/client/seedmanagement/clientset
inputs : --input seedmanagement/v1alpha1 --input seedmanagement/v1alpha1
```
As there is no directory as `github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/apis/seedmanagement/seedmanagement/v1alpha1`, it doesnot generate anything. Is it still possible to call `client-gen` on specific folder as it was done with earlier scripts?

One mitigation I can think of is to call `gen_client` function on whole `github.com/gardener/gardener/pkg/apis` and then remove the `+genclient` marker from the types for which genclient is not needed. But the issue is we won't be able to pass the `output-pkg-root` flag for each pkg.




### Why is this needed?

`gen_client()` function in `kube_codegen` script is not working as expected.

I need the scheduler to support scheduling capabilities for hardware heterogeneous scenarios, similar to the optional allocation mentioned in the DRA document.

### Why is this needed?

In the same cluster, I have multiple types of heterogeneous hardware. However, these hardware resources are difficult to unify and report as the same type through device plugins. Here are my use cases:

1. I have purchased GPUs from two different manufacturers, and they are reported as resources using device plugins on two types of nodes. However, when creating a pod, I have to explicitly declare which type of GPU resource to request, and I cannot achieve optional scheduling.

2. When assigning networking to pods, some nodes are assigned virtual network cards (virtio-pci devices), while others are assigned physical network cards (physical device). I want to achieve the scheduling effect where pods uniformly request virtio-pci network cards, and if a node doesn't have it, the pod could be scheduled to a node with a physical device.

title: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
body:
### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.



### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

title: Kubelet deletes CSI mount points if a "requiresrepublish" call to NodePublishVolume returns an error
body:
### What happened?

When a CSI driver uses `spec.requiresRepublish` to request repeated calls to NodePublishVolume, if any of the "refresh" calls return a "final" error, then Kubelet will delete the mount point on the host filesystem ([code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bdcb73d6b34288b030c5e98d6c2971fa9b074f61/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L316))

Unfortunately, doing this once the mount point has already been mounted into the target pod filesystem causes a permanent problem for the pod --- deleting the mount point from the host filesystem leaves the stale volume contents visible to the pod.  Even subsequent successful calls to NodePublishVolume don't restore the link --- the CSI driver can remount its volume in the host filesystem, but this doesn't trigger Kubelet to re-mount it into the pod filsystem.

The concrete case where I've hit this is when running a CSI driver that places auto-refreshing mTLS keys and certificates into the pod filesystem.  Refreshing the certificate requires an RPC to the issuing CA --- if this fails, and the error is bubbled up and returned from NodePublishVolume, then the target pod using the volume is stuck forever with an expired certificate.

Kubelet should either:
* Ignore errors from NodePublishVolume calls that are being used to refresh volume contents, or
* Cleanly unmount the volume on error, and remount it on the next successful call.

The first alternative probably makes more sense.

title: Unable to mount configMap below readOnly emptyDir
body:
### What happened?

ConfigMap, DownwardAPI, and Secret volumes can be mounted within each other since #60342. However, when I try to do the same with a read-only emptyDir, the container fails to start, and `runc` returns an error: `read-only file system: unknown`.

For example, this pod creates, but the container fails to start:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mount-subdirectory-issue
spec:
  containers:
    - name: main
      image: busybox
      command: [sleep, 5m]
      volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /var/my-settings
          name: one
          readOnly: true
        - mountPath: /var/my-settings/conf.d
          name: two
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: one
      emptyDir: {}
    - name: two
      configMap:
        name: two
        optional: true
```

```console
$ kubectl describe -f pod.yaml
…
    Mounts:
      /var/my-settings from one (ro)
      /var/my-settings/conf.d from two (ro)
      /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount from kube-api-access-fvv44 (ro)
Conditions:
  Type              Status
  Initialized       True
  Ready             False
  ContainersReady   False
  PodScheduled      True
Volumes:
  one:
    Type:       EmptyDir (a temporary directory that shares a pod's lifetime)
    Medium:
    SizeLimit:  <unset>
  two:
    Type:      ConfigMap (a volume populated by a ConfigMap)
    Name:      two
    Optional:  true
…
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age              From               Message
  ----     ------     ----             ----               -------
…
  Normal   Created    0s (x2 over 2s)  kubelet            Created container main
  Warning  Failed     0s (x2 over 1s)  kubelet            Error: failed to create containerd task: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed: runc create failed: unable to start container process: error during container init: error mounting "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/44d290fb-2697-4ef1-b45a-1ebb176aa70f/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap/two" to rootfs at "/var/my-settings/conf.d": mkdir /run/k3s/containerd/io.containerd.runtime.v2.task/k8s.io/main/rootfs/var/my-settings/conf.d: read-only file system: unknown
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I'm so used to arranging ConfigMap and Secret mounts in this way, I expected all ephemeral volume mounts to behave the same.

When volume `one` above is a Secret or ConfigMap, volume `two` mounts just fine.

```yaml
  volumes:
    - name: one
      configMap:
        name: one
        optional: true
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod with one container and two `emptyDir` volume mounts such that one is mounted as a subdirectory of the other.

See the example YAML above.

### Anything else we need to know?

I suspect a call to `volumeutil.MakeNestedMountpoints` around here might resolve it: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c46d737ce5ad0bb3e658736476feee41773d531d/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go#L282-L284

The runc project has an open issue to change this particular error message:
- https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/2084

title: Why eventf API of go-client requires polling
body:
Hello All,

I am referring this code and line
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/integration/events/events_test.go#L76

First I would like to thank to author for adding this example. This piece of code is really helpful to develop more complicated solution based on k8s `go-client`. But I have few questions, which arises when we go for the more complicated event posting mechanism.  

So, why polling? In a limited resource environment, when we try to send multiple events, and poll for every request, the static value 100 and 20 might not be effective, considering the load on api-server. Persistence of the sent event might take longer. Now we can argue some 99 percentile would follow this pattern, but that is not the answer. This is non-deterministic and theoretically the timeout can exceed whatever the value we set. 
So my question is, **Can we somehow modify the example so that instead of polling, some `interrupt` based mechanism would notify the caller that event has been handled to api-server for processing**.  I am not familiar with the `go-client` code that much, so I am not sure if there is any existing method/packages in `go-client` that can perform this for me. 

Thanks in advance.

title: Enable Kubelet HTTP/2 idle time configurable
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, the kubelet idle time to api server is fixed to 90 seconds. Would it be possible to make the idle time configurable, so that kubelet can recognize there is something wrong with the current connection, and reconnect sooner?   

### Why is this needed?

If there is something wrong with the connection between kubelet and api server for more than some period (40 seconds), k8s will treat nodes as not ready.

title: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
body:
### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersReady
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:20:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:20:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersReady

```

and the chain on one node only contains one of the ready endpoints:

```
KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.78.44.163/32 -p tcp -m comment --comment "svc:serviceport loadbalancer IP" -m tcp --dport 4000 -j KUBE-EXT-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43
KUBE-EXT-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 -m comment --comment "masquerade traffic for svc:serviceport external destinations" -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
KUBE-EXT-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 -j KUBE-SVC-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43
KUBE-SVC-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 ! -s 100.64.0.0/13 -d 100.72.16.186/32 -p tcp -m comment --comment "svc:serviceport cluster IP" -m tcp --dport 4000 -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
KUBE-SVC-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 -j KUBE-SEP-JDEM23RCGZCIYUJI
KUBE-SEP-JDEM23RCGZCIYUJI -s 100.64.131.130/32 -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
KUBE-SEP-JDEM23RCGZCIYUJI -p tcp -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 100.64.131.130:4000
```

this situation remains until either the pod readiness changes, a partial sync fails and it does a full resync or kube-proxy is restartet which also full syncs

The kube-proxy logs show nothing unusual, just lots of partial syncs (which in our cluster take about 1-2 seconds for a partial sync while the full sync takes 20-40seconds).

### What did you expect to happen?

On endpoint change the iptables are always configured.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We see this in clusters with 1500 services, 14000 pods and 300 nodes on most nodes for a small handful of the services.
The cluster is running v1.26.9
I have written a very crude script to check for the inconsistencies and fix them via a proxy restart:
https://gist.github.com/juliantaylor/996e0255809cb2077b66dc034ec47f55
I imagine reproducing it is tricky, but maybe someone can run the script in their clusters maybe also in a newer version to see is still a problem.
Note due to races it can report errors while stuff in the cluster is changing, but if a deployment behind an ip is stable and still shows up kube-proxy has not configured it properly. (One could at a check on the ready state transition time in the script to avoid this)

```
./check-iptables-nodes.sh $(kubectl get nodes | awk '{print $1}'

kworker-be-prod-iz2-003

### What happened?

This is a follow up to investigate and potentially fix based on this comment: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120731#pullrequestreview-1689842503.

The values for `CurrentReplicas` and `UpdatedReplicas` in status fields are invalid. 

### What did you expect to happen?

Quoting the comment:

There's still issue of the mismatching statuses, as I explained in slack, but I'll also post here for visibility:

While testing this PR I found STS status isn't also fully correct, I started logging out full status right after each wait command and I'm seeing this:

```
// CurrentRevision is the only revision, and the CurrentReplicas matches Replicas, ie. 3
STEP: 1: Status v1.StatefulSetStatus{ObservedGeneration:1, Replicas:3, ReadyReplicas:3, CurrentReplicas:3, UpdatedReplicas:3, CurrentRevision:"ss2-7b6c9599d5", UpdateRevision:"ss2-7b6c9599d5", AvailableReplicas:3}
// after first update, with Partition=1, we need to update only 2 pods (1 and 2), but CurrentReplicas (ie. old) should be 0, UpdatedReplicas (ie. new) should be 2
STEP: 2: Status v1.StatefulSetStatus{ObservedGeneration:2, Replicas:3, ReadyReplicas:3, CurrentReplicas:2, UpdatedReplicas:0, CurrentRevision:"ss2-7b6c9599d5", UpdateRevision:"ss2-5459d8585b", AvailableReplicas:3}
// after the pod removal, we need to recreate the pod for CurrentRevision, so CurrentReplicas=1, and UpdatedReplicas=2
STEP: 3: Status v1.StatefulSetStatus{ObservedGeneration:2, Replicas:3, ReadyReplicas:3, CurrentReplicas:1, UpdatedReplicas:2, CurrentRevision:"ss2-7b6c9599d5", UpdateRevision:"ss2-5459d8585b", AvailableReplicas:3}
if one checks the descriptions we have in [our API]
```

(https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/b01b44926aa4920c8c8c008003e16316cf59ffda/apps/v1/types.go#L276-L296) we clearly are doing a bad job reflecting the actual changes happening to Current(Replicas|Revision) and Updated(Replicas|Revisions) such that they don't reflect the actual state of world, since the division between Current and Updated should be strictly tied to Partitions (as described in [the original proposal](https://github.com/kubernetes/design-proposals-archive/blob/main/apps/statefulset-update.md)).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the e2e test with logging of the status: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120731#pullrequestreview-1689842503.

title: Server side apply increments resource version for certain fields every second
body:
### What happened?

I server-side applied an object many times.  It has no changes, so should not write anything. Instead, everytime the write is in a new second, it writes. Multiple writes in the same second are correctly ignored.

/sig api-machinery

### What did you expect to happen?

 It has no changes, so should not write anything.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a cluster. I reproduced this on:

* kind v1.28.0
* kind v1.29.0-alpha.2
* GKE 1.28.1

I didn't try any other versions

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: default
spec:

  listeners:

    port: 443
    protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      certificateRefs:
      - name: test
      mode: Terminate
```

Working:
```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: echo
  namespace: default
spec:
  gatewayClassName: test
  listeners:
  - name: test
    port: 443
    protocol: HTTP
```

This portion of the CRD: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/blob/cdc85ca46615905238674c535239cac163c21c13/config/crd/standard/gateway.networking.k8s.io_gateways.yaml#L395.

Messing with the CRD, I can reduce it to exactly what triggers the issue:
```yaml
tls:
  properties:
    certificateRefs:
      items:
        properties:
          group:
            default: X # THIS BREAKS IT
            type: string
          kind:
            type: string
          name:
            type: string
          namespace:
            type: string
        required:
        - name
        type: object
      maxItems: 64
      type: array
    mode:
      default: Terminate
      enum:
      - Terminate
      - Passthrough
      type: string
  type: object
```

If I explicitly set the field, instead of relying on the defaulting, it works fine.

Maybe related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115563

title: When Pod fails to schedule during bind stage, PVC and PV are still bound, prevent pod reschedule to another node
body:
### What happened?

In my cluster, I have three nodes, each belonging to different availability zones: us-east-1a, us-east-1b, and us-east-1c. I have a StatefulSet resource with a replica count of 3, set podManagementPolicy as Parallel to allow creating pods in parallel. The StatefulSet resource uses volumeClaimTemplate to declare the use of persistent storage. To ensure that the three pods are scheduled in different zones, I've also configured the topologySpreadConstraints.

When kube-scheduler decides to schedule pod-A to node-1(assume pod in kube-scheduler's cache), kube-scheduler will add an annotation `volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node: node-1` on PVC to notify external provisioner to create PV and bound with PVC for pod-A.

The problem is sometimes pod-A scheduling fails at bind stage for some reason. kube-scheduler removes the assumed pod-A from cache, and adds it to the backoff queue for rescheduling, **but PV and PVC for pod-A remain bound to the node and won't be cleaned up.**

The next pod, pod-B, is then scheduled and happens to be assigned to the same node, without considering that the previous pod-A had already created a PVC and PV on that node. Pod-B successfully schedules on node-1. 

**When it's time to reschedule pod-A, it's unable to schedule to another node because pod-A's PVC is already bound to node-1. Furthermore, due to topologySpreadConstraints limits, pod-A cannot be scheduled to the same node (node-1) as pod-B**. As a result, pod-A remains in pending state forever. Even if I add new nodes to the cluster later, pod-A still won't be scheduled to other nodes. Currently, the only solution is to delete pod-A and PVC-A so that pod-A can be rescheduled to a different node.

Here is the StatefulSet definition.

title: Kubelet not create Symlink for configmap volume after restarted
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet is creating configmap volume  for a pod, it finished writing `timestamp` dir and made symlink to `..data`. At the same time, the kubelet is restarted, unfortunately the configmap item symlink is not created.

The restarted kubelet will try to `SetUpAt` configmap,  `no update required for target directory`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should create absent symlink for configmap volume.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. We can hack kubelet to help reproduce it: sleep some time before `createUserVisibleFiles` https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...chenk008:kubernetes:test_kubelet_configmap_writer`
2. stop kubelet and start official kubelet
3. kubelet will skip to create symlink for UserVisibleFiles

title: daemonset pod cannot be created quickly, when some nodes are added to the cluster and controller-manager OOM will be triggered
body:
### What happened? ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112319 【Question】 question 1: Now our k8s cluster has 5k nodes. When we expand some nodes in the k8s cluster, the daemonset pod cannot be created quickly. It takes about 2 hours to create the daemonset pod. Add a new node daemonset pod startup time: ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/ef2d7885-1ce4-4e90-9340-205b00093f5f) ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/5b0e4cb4-1fa2-470e-8eea-bb6e92c1002d) question 2: Look at the monitoring of `kube-controller-manager` Memory usage reaches 900GB and triggers OOM. `kube-controller-manager` memory usage monitoring: ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/6b628b11-1676-4862-9616-07f99554ce36) 【Solution】 In a cluster with 5K nodes, we found that when the daemonset controller watches update `Node` events, due to the large number of `Node` events, the `NodeInformer` [pendingNotifications](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e438c54a77ccf7b9e0aff924eb977031099cc2f/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L876) ring buffer has more `Node` events to be processed, resulting in the Node EventHandler's `Add/Update` callback function being processed slowly. Affects the creation of daemonset pod and `kube-controller-manager` `OOM` issues. We optimized the [shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1d9e1e6d56cbd5c9d04ba25cccf184a973056a79/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L693) logic in the [UpdateNode](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1d9e1e6d56cbd5c9d04ba25cccf184a973056a79/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L693) method of the daemonset controller `NodeInformer` to reduce unnecessary Node event processing: original code: ``` func shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate(oldNode, curNode v1.Node) bool { if !nodeInSameCondition(oldNode.Status.Conditions, curNode.Status.Conditions) { return false } oldNode.ResourceVersion = curNode.ResourceVersion oldNode.Status.Conditions = curNode.Status.Conditions return apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldNode, curNode) } ``` optimized code: ``` func shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate(oldNode, curNode v1.Node) bool { if !nodeInSameCondition(oldNode.Status.Conditions, curNode.Status.Conditions) { return false } oldNode.ResourceVersion = curNode.ResourceVersion oldNode.Status.Conditions = curNode.Status.Conditions + oldNode.Status.Images = curNode.Status.Images + oldNode.Status.NodeInfo = curNode.Status.NodeInfo + oldNode.Status.Capacity = curNode.Status.Capacity + oldNode.Status.Allocatable = curNode.Status.Allocatable return apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldNode, curNode) } func (dsc *DaemonSetsController) updateNode(old, cur interface{}) { oldNode := old.(*v1.Node) curNode := cur.(*v1.Node) + oldNodeCopy := oldNode.DeepCopy() + curNodeCopy := curNode.DeepCopy() if shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate(*oldNodeCopy, *curNodeCopy) { return } dsList, err := dsc.dsLister.List(labels.Everything()) if err != nil { klog.V(4).Infof("Error listing daemon sets: %v", err) return } // TODO: it'd be nice to pass a hint with these enqueues, so that each ds would only examine the added node (unless it has other work to do, too). for _, ds := range dsList { _, oldShouldSchedule, oldShouldContinueRunning, err := dsc.nodeShouldRunDaemonPod(oldNode, ds) if err != nil { klog.Errorf("Error old node %s should run daemon %s/%s pod: %v", oldNode.Name, ds.Namespace, ds.Name, err) continue } _, currentShouldSchedule, currentShouldContinueRunning, err := dsc.nodeShouldRunDaemonPod(curNode, ds) if err != nil { klog.Errorf("Error current node %s should run daemon %s/%s pod: %v", oldNode.Name, ds.Namespace, ds.Name, err) continue } if (oldShouldSchedule != currentShouldSchedule) || (oldShouldContinueRunning != currentShouldContinueRunning) { klog.V(4).Infof("enqueueing daemon set %s/%s for node %v.", ds.Namespace, ds.Name, curNode.Name) dsc.enqueueDaemonSet(ds) } } } ``` 【Effect】 After adding some nodes to the cluster, the daemonset pod can be quickly created, and the `kube-controller-manager` memory is controlled at about 20GB. ![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/3377677/5c9e3a0a-13ac-45c6-b722-d8a1c802b14b) ### What did you expect to happen? 1. When adding some nodes to the k8s cluster, daemonset pod can be created quickly because the node requires CNI daemonset pod. 2. kube-controller-manager needs to use less memory to prevent frequent `OOM`triggers. 3. We have optimized the `shouldIgnoreNodeUpdate` logic in the `updateNode` method of the daemonset controller `NodeInformer` to reduce unnecessary `Node `event processing. Is this optimization logic possible? ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? When the k8s cluster size reaches 5k, add new nodes to the cluster. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"17+", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"17+", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} ```

title: Custom resource objects can be created during CRD Termination using server-side apply
body:
### What happened?

After a CRD DELETE, while the CRD finalizer is deleting all custom resource objects of that type, and the `Terminating=True` status condition is set, it should not be possible to create objects of that type, but it is with server-side apply, because the creation prevention implementation blocks by method type and there's no check in the PATCH handler.

- CREATE is blocked: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/customresource_handler.go#L373
- PATCH is not blocked: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/customresource_handler.go#L390

In the Patch Apply handler, the `forceAllowCreate` flag is set to `true`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/patch.go#L646 This allows patching to always create objects.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the CRD is terminating, SSA should not be able to create new objects.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. apply a CRD
2. apply a CR with a manual finalizer to block CRD termination
3. delete the CRD
4. create a new CR with SSA

### Anything else we need to know?

There is another race condition allowing creation, but it's otherwise unrelated to this bug, which is not a race condition: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/99181

title: Define new well-known annotation: `kubernetes.io/display-name`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

~~We~~ VMware would like to define a new, well-known annotation, `kubernetes.io/display-name`, per [_Well-known labels, annotations, and taints_](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints). A quick tl;dr about the history of this issue is as follows:

* There is a PR open at https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/43658.
* This topic has been discussed in [this thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C5P3FE08M/p1697837862269049) in the `#sig-architecture` channel from k8s Slack.
* @sftim has been a giant help in shepherding this issue.
* @dims requested this issue be filed and assigned to `#sig-cli`.

/sig cli

### Why is this needed?

To my knowledge, such an annotation does not exist, and while [`kubernetes.io/description`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#description) is close, it is not exactly the same thing. ~~We~~ VMware was likely to introduce a similar annotation internally due to the lack of a standard, well-known annotation for this use case in upstream K8s. However, after speaking with some folks, we opted to [engage](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C1J0BPD2M/p1697816976615399) `#sig-docs`, who suggested we [reach out](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C5P3FE08M/p1697837862269049) to `#sig-architecture` about adding this annotation to upstream K8.

#### Goals

1. **Standard approach for mutable, human-readable name on K8s objects**
  Users & non-interactive processes should be able to read/write a K8s object's human-readable name.

1. **Well-defined syntax and character set for human-readable names**
  Users & non-interactive processes should be able to read/write human-readable names using UTF-16.

1. **Support for human-readable name in standard human-readable column**
  Applications that surface or present K8s objects should be able to refer to a common location for surfacing an object's human-readable name.

#### Non-goals

1. **Object relationships based on human-readable names**
  Support for defining relationships between objects based on their human-readable names is not in scope of this change. Object relationships must still be defined using an object's name.

1. **Performant query/search for objects based on human-readable names**
  Support for performant queries based on human-readable names is not in scope of this change. Server-side indexing/filtering of objects is not supported by annotations, only labels. While both labels and annotations offer mutability, the former's values are constrained to a restrictive character set. The ability to input free-form data for a human-readable name was prioritized over searching for objects based on human-readable names.

1. **Support for human-readable names built into `kubectl`**
  Support for this annotation in `kubectl` is not in scope of this change. APIs may use this annotation's value as an additional printer column to surface this annotation's value when printing objects with `kubectl`. However, any feature such as the introduction of a `--display-name` flag to print the human-readable names for objects is not part of this change.

title: Topology Aware Routing's OverloadThreshold should be configurable per Service
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently OverloadThreshold is defined as a float constant:

```
const (
        // OverloadThreshold represents the maximum overload any individual endpoint
        // should be exposed to.
        OverloadThreshold float64 = 0.2
)
```

Instead it should be configurable per each service that has the annotation enabling TAR.

### Why is this needed?

There are valid use cases which could benefit from topology-aware routing, but they cannot, because the hardcoded value of OverloadThreshold is too conservative.

Consider a 3-node instance group dedicated to loki. There is one node per availability zone. There are 3 pods that receive incoming traffic:

```
loki-write-0                  1/1     Running   0             28h
loki-write-1                  1/1     Running   0             10h
loki-write-2                  1/1     Running   0             29h
```

Since the pods have pod anti-affinity, each of them runs on its own node, each of which is launched in its own availability zone.

It is desirable to send traffic from clients in the same AZ to the respective loki-write pod running in that AZ to save on cross-zone traffic expenses. Topology aware routing could be a solution, but, alas, KCM tells the following:

```
type: 'Warning' reason: 'TopologyAwareHintsDisabled' Unable to allocate minimum required endpoints to each zone without exceeding overload threshold (3 endpoints, 3 zones), addressType: IPv4
```

In this case, even if all traffic goes to a single pod, it will still be acceptable, because the pods are very far from CPU saturation, and a single pod can easily take full load. 3 pods in this case are needed purely for HA reasons and not load distribution.

Having configurable OverloadThreshold would solve the problem here.

Another solution would be to implement support for `internalTrafficPolicy: PreferLocal`, which has been discussed a lot, but changing the hardcoded value of OverloadThreshold to a variable that can be set via a Service annotation seems to be a significantly easier job.

There is also a possible workaround: deploy a sufficient number of trivial proxy pods, the number being a multiple of 3, that will be divided into 3 groups, each having required inter-pod affinities to run on the same node or in the same AZ as the respective loki-write-N pod, and configured to forward incoming traffic to that pod via a headless service. Then create a Service with topology aware routing enabled to send traffic to these X*3 pods to trick KCM into thinking that there is now a sufficient number of endpoints to prevent overload.

But it's an ugly solution. Something more elegant is long due. Users need to be able to say "I know what I'm doing, just keep traffic in the same node (AZ), unless there is no available endpoint, in which case fall back to other node, then other AZ" in a simple way.

title: JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX is bound too late for env var expansion
body:
### What happened?

I was trying to rename the `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` environment variable to the name my job container was expecting, e.g.:

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: job-foo
spec:
  parallelism: 1
  completions: 1
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: foo
          image: debian:bookworm
          command: ["/bin/sh"]
          args:
            - "-c"
            - |
              echo $JOB_ID
              echo $JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX
          env:
            - name: JOB_ID
              value: $(JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX)
```

However, it appears that `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` is added to the environment variables _after_ the normal processing, because it's not expanded properly in the `env` declaration:

```
$ kubectl logs job-foo-0-j94lb
$(JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX)
0
```

This conclusion appears to be reinforced by the fact that `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` is added to the end of the environment variables map:

```

title: Existing scheduler-extender framework transfer too much content, which resulting in the poor performance in production K8s clusters when new pod needs to be scheduled
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When I write a scheduler extender in my k8s cluster, try to extend one extend policy to let k8s scheduler take my extender into consideration, while found that:

#### the content of [extenderv1.ExtenderArgs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.28/pkg/scheduler/extender.go#L256C1-L256C38) that need to be sent is too large, which make the  performance so poor for each pod's scheduling.

Why we did not just send the nodeName list by default, and then let each scheduler extender to watch-list the node contents and pods, and then return the result, just like [what Prioritize does: just return a nodeName list and score](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/extender.go#L319)?

I see the issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/72634 was already discussing about it, but seems there is no actions in upstream.

kind/feature


## What did you expect to happen? ## 

For scheduler extender framework, just send the content as small as possible, let each scheduler-extender watch-list get the contents from api-server or something else.

Kubernetes version
v1.23 and master

k8s Cluster node number
5000

Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)
N/A

Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)
CNI




### Why is this needed?

Existing scheduler-extender framework is a very brilliant design for incoming-scheduler extender! It did not affect any other components to achieve the extendable features.

While in reality, after adding such extender, the time cost is several times that of the original. it depends on the scale of k8s clusters, when there are more than 5000 nodes in one clusters, the result is the disaster.

One of the main reasons is that "there are too much content to transfer between scheduler-extender framework and users scheduler-extender".

are there some concern that we did not send the [full-nodelist contents](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.28/pkg/scheduler/extender.go#L256C1-L256C38) for scheduler-extender framework? why not just send the nodelist ??

title: Can’t connect from Pods on one server to Pods on different server using VXLAN
body:
### What happened?

I build Kubernetes cluster v1.26.9 on Virtual Machines with RHEL 8.6. I am using flannel as Container Networking Interface with backend VXLAN. Communication between Pods on the same server works fine but I can’t connect from Pods on one server to Pods on different server.

For testing purposes I tried to use flannel with UDP backend. It helped. Connection between Pods on different servers is possible when UDP backend is used. Since UDP backend is recommended only for debugging, it can't be my final solution. That is why I want to configure connection using VXLAN.

I also tried to configure connection using host-gw backend but it also didn't work.

There is no firewall between servers. Connection between servers is possible.
Firewalld service is disabled on servers.
SELinux is set to permissive.
In sysctl below options are set:
    net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
    net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
    net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1
    net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-arptables = 1
In /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf there are set options:
    overlay
    br_netfilter
Execution of command "iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT" didn't help.
Reboot of VMs didn't help.



### What did you expect to happen?

It is possible to connect from Pods on one server to Pods on different server for flannel with VXLAN backend.





### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: Statefulset scales out wrong pods with partition
body:
### What happened?

I have a statefulset with `replicas=4` and `partition=2`. After updating podTemplate to change the image fields, two old version pods and two new version pods are presented. 
Then scale down the statefulset to 0, and scale it up to 2, the 2 newly created pods are of the new version, which is not the expected behavior.

Possible solution: check whether the replicas is zero before changing `currentRevision`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d0084356b3cabdafcfc140d19ad8d544b2fc9b5d/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go#L583 They should be processed correctly then.

### What did you expect to happen?

After updating the statefulset, scale it down to 0, then scale up to 2, two old version pods should be created, because the partition is 2.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- create a statefulset with replicas=4 and partition=2
- update the image field of the statefulset
- 2 old version pods and 2 new verison pods are presented
- scale down the replicas to 0
- scale up the replicas to 2
- 2 pods of new version are created, which are unexpected

title: Env variable is missing in container, after cleanup of duplications in deployment
body:
### What happened?

Unintentionally we defined the same env twice in our deployment.
```
          env:
          - name: PARAMETER
            value: "example"
          - name: PARAMETER
            value: "example"
```
The deployment itself has worked and the env in container was available.
Later, we cleaned it up - simply removed the duplicated entry
```
          env:
          - name: PARAMETER
            value: "example"
```
After deployment, the application broke, because the env was not available in the affected container.
After we deployed it again, the variable was set again

### What did you expect to happen?

After the cleanup, the env variable must still be set in the container because it is still defined in the deployment.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```console
kubectl create ns env-issue

kubectl apply -n env-issue -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: env-issue-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.20
          env:
          - name: FOO
            value: "bar"
          - name: PARAMETER
            value: "example"
          - name: PARAMETER
            value: "example"
EOF


kubectl -n env-issue describe deployment.apps/env-issue-deployment

title: Endpoints and EndpointSlices can have duplicate addresses with different Ready conditions
body:
both Endpoints and EndpointSlices can contain the same IP duplicate with different Condition. In case of Endpoints this means the same IP is at the same time Ready and NotReady, leaving to implementations how to best deal with it.

This was not a problem in the past for Endpoints, before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94112, because the kube-apiserver canonicalized the Endpoints using the RepackSubsets function https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ea5e4bc2326c71250774f6a4f5545492c5621760/pkg/api/v1/endpoints/util_test.go#L206-L221 , removing the duplication.

This patch just adds two unit tests to document this and verify that we maintain the existing behavior, since does not sound likely we strict validation now not allowing IPs to be duplicated.


I just found out about this while debugging https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121231#issuecomment-1763245731

```
kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -o yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Endpoints
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"v1","kind":"Endpoints","metadata":{"annotations":{},"labels":{"endpointslice.kubernetes.io/skip-mirror":"true"},"name":"kubernetes","namespace":"default"},"subsets":[{"addresses":[{"ip":"192.168.8.4"}],"ports":[{"name":"https","port":6443,"protocol":"TCP"}]},{"notReadyAddresses":[{"ip":"192.168.8.4"}],"ports":[{"name":"https","port":6443,"protocol":"TCP"}]}]}
  creationTimestamp: "2023-10-12T16:22:09Z"
  labels:
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/skip-mirror: "true"
  name: kubernetes
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "854537"
  uid: c6a8f3b3-afbe-48e6-89c3-2b27d4284c5d
subsets:
- addresses:
  - ip: 192.168.8.4
  ports:
  - name: https
    port: 6443
    protocol: TCP
- notReadyAddresses:
  - ip: 192.168.8.4
  ports:
  - name: https
    port: 6443
    protocol: TCP
```


### Notes from original discussion

              While it's possible to have 2 EPS and thereby have duplicate endpoints, I think we should still consider validating no dups within a slice.  Lots of use-cases have just one slice (by design!)

_Originally posted by @thockin in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121330#issuecomment-1773290647_

title: The e2e CI test for the Garbage collector in sig-api-machinery is reporting an error
body:
### What happened?

Kubernetes e2e suite: [It] [sig-api-machinery] Garbage collector should support orphan deletion of custom resources [sig-api-machinery]

As stated in https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/util/wait/poll.go#L84:
```
// Deprecated: This method does not return errors from context, use PollUntilContextTimeout.
// Note that the new method will no longer return ErrWaitTimeout and instead return errors
// defined by the context package. Will be removed in a future release.
func PollWithContext(ctx context.Context, interval, timeout time.Duration, condition ConditionWithContextFunc) error {
	return poll(ctx, false, poller(interval, timeout), condition)

title: Correct Keyword name for DisruptionsAllowed in PDB.
body:
When describing a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) in text, JSON, or YAML format, the keyword used to represent the "Number of pod disruptions that are currently allowed" should ideally be `disruptionsAllowed`. This naming convention is more consistent with the typical JSON/YAML key naming practices. It not only adheres to the convention but also clearly conveys its meaning. Using `disruptionsAllowed` makes it instantly clear that it defines the allowed number of disruptions.

Furthermore, consistent naming practices in JSON and YAML are essential for clarity and maintainability. When key names align with their meaning, it becomes easier for humans and automated systems to understand and work with the data. This consistency helps reduce potential confusion and errors in managing resources like PodDisruptionBudgets in a Kubernetes cluster.

For example, a PodDisruptionBudget configuration in YAML format might look like this:

```yaml

apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  disruptionsAllowed: 1
 ```
By using `disruptionsAllowed` as the keyword, it is clear that this PDB allows only one disruption while keeping a minimum of two pods available. This naming convention helps maintain readability and understanding in the Kubernetes configuration.

title: Kube-Proxy IPVS mode support port hash and fallback in sh schedule
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Current `sh` load balancing policy only performs hashing of sourcing IP, the server load maybe really high when only a single client is sending bunch of data to the server; So like this MR, we definitely need source port hash flag in `sh` policy as well

Another things is the `sh` don't have the fallback flag enabled, which the client will have no endpoints to send when the hashed one is unready and the weight set to zero. Can refer to this [patch](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20130619095425.GA20145@eldamar.org.uk/)

### Why is this needed?

kubeproxy IPVS mod should include src-port hash and fallback flag in  `sh` policy.

title: Allowed configure IPVS scheduler per service
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The ipvs scheduler is configured by clusters, can we allow it to be configured by service?

For our situation is we configure the `rr` for the cluster, all the node will pick the first the same apiserver since server list is well sorted, so when we create a daemonset with all newly started apiserver, the daemonset will direct to the first apiserver which will cause a lot load to it and cause it OOM cuz the list request is quite expensive. If we change cluster configuration to `sh` or `mh`, it will influence the other request like there is a client on single node and rely on service loadbalancing.

### Why is this needed?

Allowed configure IPVS scheduler per service

title: SharedIndexInformer not calling event handlers during the first resync
body:
This issue is the root cause for https://github.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/issues/10947

Based on my tests, the issue was introduced between client-go `v0.24.0-alpha.1` and `v0.24.0-alpha.2`.

Seems like when the first resync happens (20 minutes in case of argo-workflows), the event handlers are not being called.

I was able to identify a potential change that introduced this: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/54928eef9f824667b23a938188498992d437156a#diff-dbac68d65bbc9814c2336df6ee91f22e807d84a9127a4d34a8b39c5657d0e447L551

Looking at the code, there is small behavior change when evaluating the isSync flag:
- resource version was checked only when `d.Type == Replaced`. Now it's being evaluated on all updates
- the `d.Type == Sync` set the isSync to true
- for any other cases: isSync is false

All an in one, there might be a chance of falsely setting isSync to true.

This flag is being used in `distribute`, which conditionally calls the listeners.

The issue also reproduces with latest client-go version: v0.29.0-alpha.2

title: Dualstack Service endpoints are only from one IP family

For a dualstack Service, its endpoints are only from one IP family.
```
	if len(svc.Spec.IPFamilies) > 0 {

Treat each IPv4/IPv6 address as separate, distinct endpoints, and include each address in the comma-separated list of addresses in an 'Endpoints' API object.

Given a phased approach, the 2 single-family endpoint approach represents the least disruptive change. Services will select only the endpoints that match the spec.ipFamily defined in the Service.

title: RBAC return 403 Forbidden after restarting APIServer when there is a large amount of
body:
### What happened?

Pod access APIServer normal at beginning, but after restarting APIServer, the access returns 403 in a few minutes at the begining of APIServer became ready.

`"HTTP" verb="GET" URI="/api/v1/namespaces/nsxxx/configmaps?resourceVersion=970285583&allowWatchBookmarks=true&watch=true" latency="1.097754946s" userAgent="xxx" srcIP="xxx" resp=403 contentType="application/json" requestID="xxx"`


### What did you expect to happen?

The access returns 200 after APIServer become ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

First create over fifty thousand rolebindings in the same namespace, then use one role in that namespace access apiserver with RBAC authorization will return 200.
At this point, restart the APIServer and access it immediately after it is running, then apiserver will return 403.

### Anything else we need to know?

I debug the code of rbac and found during authorization, APIServer would list all rolebindings in the informer to find the role binding to user. However, at the beginning of startup, due to the large number of rolebindings, the informer was not yet fully synced, so cannot find the role binding to the request user, then return 403.
I think the APISever should wait for rbac versionedInformers cache sync before serving.

title: apiserver admission plugins should zero-copy k8s objects
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like apiserver admission plugins to reference k8s objects from the [storage](https://github.com/kubernetes/apiserver/blob/v0.28.3/pkg/registry/rest/rest.go#L55) rather than using informers to [fetch](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubeapiserver/options/authentication.go#L613) objects from itself.

### Why is this needed?

Informers fetching objects from apiserver itself not only causes CPU overhead for apiserver to process the requests but also effectively results in a copy of all k8s objects inside kube-apiserver process, which can be optimized if we could find a way to reference those objects by pointers from [storage](https://github.com/kubernetes/apiserver/blob/v0.28.3/pkg/registry/rest/rest.go#L55)

title: Reduce the daemonset controller Node event-handler code logic to avoid the callback function processing Node events too slowly.
body:
### What happened?

issue ref:https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121474#issuecomment-1786835345

When the daemonset controller watches update Node events, due to the large number of Node events, the `NodeInformer` [pendingNotifications](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e438c54a77ccf7b9e0aff924eb977031099cc2f/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L876) ring buffer has more Node events to be processed, resulting in the Node EventHandler's Add/Update callback function being processed slowly.

### What did you expect to happen?

 We should rewrite the daemonset controller to the pattern where event-handler is as cheap as possible by simply putting stuff into queue. The queue then gives us deduplication for free and all the logic is then happening in the workers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

When the cluster size is 5K, the daemonset pod cannot be quickly created on the node.

title: Job readiness gates
body:
### What would you like to be added?

An alternative to `Job.spec.suspend` that allows multiple controllers to cooperate towards starting a Job.

This is analogous to scheduling gates https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-scheduling-readiness/

### Why is this needed?

This would enable queueing of steps of a workflow.

For example, the job could have:
```
readinessGates:
  - kueue.k8s.io/suspend
  - snakemake.io/step
```

The job is only allowed to run (create pods) if all gates are removed.
In the case above, `snakemake.io/step` would be removed by snakemake when all the dependencies for this job are completed.

At this point, kueue would allow this job to compete for resources in the queue. When there is enough quota to run this job, Kueue would remove the `kueue.k8s.io/suspend`.

title: ReplicaSet naming is inconsistent
body:
### What happened?

When kubernetes is creating a ReplicaSet automatically through a deployment, the suffix added to the deployment name has an inconsistent length. Although this is not necessarily a bug, this can lead to issues in trying to identify ReplicaSets that were created through deployments using, for instance, RegEx.

[This code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9754e404390a8d4e969e17e339586376b6f6ad8f/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L1201) is responsible for creating a suffix string to add to the deployment name to create the ReplicaSet name. The number created by `podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()` is any number from 0 to 4,294,967,295. This means the suffix string after the number goes through `rand.SafeEncodeString` ([link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/rand/rand.go#L121)) will have a length of 0 to 10.

### What did you expect to happen?

ReplicaSet names should always have a suffix of consistent length when created automatically via a deployment.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a number of deployments that will in turn create ReplicaSets. On average, 23% of these ReplicaSets will have suffixes of length 9 or shorter instead of the expected 10.

### Anything else we need to know?

An easy solution would be to simply change the code as follows:
```
return rand.SafeEncodeString(fmt.Sprintf("%0*d", 10, podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()))
```
There is no risk to a solution like this as it will only go into effect when new ReplicaSet revisions are created and will only make ReplicaSet names more consistent. Any names that would be generated out of a number like 1,234,567 will instead be generated by 0,001,234,567, i.e. there is the same number of possible suffixes as before.

### Kubernetes version

Doesn't really matter but:
```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.28.0
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp: lookup ...: no such host
```


### Cloud provider

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Due to transient issues with the infrastructure sometimes the docker image pull fails and in the current version of Kubernetes there is no ability to retry the Docker image pull when it fails due to transient issues such as Network issues. At present this is handled manually where the production support person will do a retry of it.

### Why is this needed?

1. Reduce the Turn around time 
2.  Replace manual effort in retrying

title: How to access app  in k8s cluster by aggregator apiservice with Authorization header
body:
I deployed a third-party web application in the k8s cluster with deployment+service. The web application mainly provides login verification api  and other web service api. After calling the login api, Bearer token will be responsed, and be set into Authorization Bearer token before calling other web service api. It works well when requests are from k8s cluster inside.


This k8s cluster has a public IP, but strict firewall rules and security group rules are set up. Only port 6443 is exposed to the public network, and additional ports are not allowed. I am wondering if there is any way to access the web app in the cluster through the public IP+6443 port of the k8s cluster.


I found the k8s aggregator apiservice. After creating the apiservice and pointing it to my web service,  running  `curl -X POST --cacert ./ca.crt --cert ./client.crt --key . /client.key -H "contentType: application/json" -d '{username: xx, password: yy}' https://ip:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/services/my-svc:port-80/proxy/api/login` is success, and the Bearer token is responsed, but I run (`curl -X POST --cacert ./ca.crt - -cert ./client.crt --key ./client.key -H "contentType: application/json" -H '{Authorization: Bearer xxx}' https://ip:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/services/my-svc:port-80/proxy/api/other-api`) to request other api, it returns 401 Unauthorized . I suspect that the header in request was intercepted or consumed by kube-apiserver, and was not passed to my web app.

Here is my question: 1. Is there any other way to access the applications in the cluster through the public IP + 6443 port of the k8s cluster? 2. How can I access the applications in the cluster without changing the firewall and security group rules or the third-party application source code, just using the Authorization Bearer toker header through kube-apiserver to complete the authentication?

### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120780 recently merged, adding nodes as something we can put in bound object refs (yay!)

title: Default settings for EvictionHard do not include imagesfs.inodesFree.
body:
It is possible to deploy Kubernetes with a separate filesystem.  We default the settings for EvictionHard [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/master/pkg/kubelet/eviction/defaults_linux.go).

A concern is that if users are using the default settings and separate filesystem for images, we are effectively turning off monitoring for INodes on the imagefs.  This means that we won't have disk pressure if inodes run out on the ImageFs.  

The fix can be to add 

```
var DefaultEvictionHard = map[string]string{
	"memory.available":  "100Mi",
	"nodefs.available":  "10%",
	"nodefs.inodesFree": "5%",
	"imagefs.available": "15%",
        "imagefs.inodesFree": "5%",
}
```
To default settings.

This doesn't seem to be a regression as these defaults were added 5 years ago (k8s 1.12) but this could be a potential bug if either users mount a separate filesystem to their container runtime storage or they configure their runtime to store their images on a separate filesystem.

title: Set enableServiceLinks to false as default
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I want to make enableServiceLinks disabled by default.

### Why is this needed?

Service link environment variables are injected into every pod. It creates three environment variables for every service in a respective pod's namespace, regardless of how they are related. This behavior was observed in EKS 1.24.

In larger namespaces, this can cause pods to crash due to too many environmental variables. I assume this is due to Container runtime or Operating System Limitations.

I assume this was needed for legacy network reasons or installs that do not run cluster DNS. Regardless, Cluster DNS is added by default for most Kubernetes installers (excluding mircok8s) out there today.

I am willing to contribute if this is the direction we want to go.

title: HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS+HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS > 40s will cause all node NotReady
body:
### What happened?

The controller-manager node-lifecycle-controller watches node lease and update `nodeHealthMap` probeTimestamp , and it check node probeTimestamp is before `now - node-monitor-grace-period`. The node-monitor-grace-period default value is 40s.

When the client connection lost, the lease watcher cannot receive new event. With the http2 health check,   HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default is 30s, HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default is  15s, it will delay 45s to kill http2  connection.  

During this period, node-lifecycle-controller will mark all nodes NotReady.

Here are some logs

```
I1103 23:00:28.464015       1 node_lifecycle_controller.go:1097] node 10.0.10.240 hasn't been updated for 40.010894415s. Last Ready is: &NodeCondition{Type:Ready,Status:True,LastHeartbeatTime:2023-11-03 22:57:18 +0800 CST,LastTransitionTime:2023-04-21 14:39:17 +0800 CST,Reason:KubeletReady,Message:kubelet is posting ready status,}

W1103 23:00:41.408493       1 reflector.go:441] k8s.io/client-go/informers/factory.go:134: watch of *v1.Lease ended with: an error on the server ("unable to decode an event from the watch stream: http2: client connection lost") has prevented the request from succeeding
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When the http2 connection lost, the watch should stop as soon as possible. The reflector should relist resource, and node-lifecycle-controller should not mark all node NotReady.

HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS+HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS should be less than 40s.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Find the controller-manager node-lifecycle-controller watch client srcIP:srcPort. Drop all tcp package send into srcIP:srcPort.
2. Wait for more than 40 seconds, all node will be marked NotReady
3. All node will be Ready after some seconds.

title: Use watch connection to get old leases in leader election
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Maintain a watch connection to synchronize the lease with kube-apiserver instead of [getting](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/leaderelection/resourcelock/leaselock.go#L42) the lease via a GET request 

### Why is this needed?

Every time a leader election client tries to update lease, it needs to get the old lease first to check identify and time, which has a few issues:

* APF concurrent share for leader election by default is quite low (i.e. 10), it could be too small in small machines hosting kube-apiserver. Using watch connection would reduce 50% leader election requests.
* Getting lease without specifying `resourceVersion` takes slight more resource from `kube-apiserver` to serve. When under load, `kube-apiserver` might be failed to response within timeout.

One major risk of doing is the client may get stale leases and decide to take the lease. I haven't looked into the code of handing lease PUT requests, but I think it should be taken care of to avoid giving up lease prematurely since there is not guarantee about freshness of GET response anyway.

title: Log a warning if Kubelet is configured with a separate filesystem but imagefs.available and imagefs.inodesfree evictionHard are not set
body:
### What would you like to be added?

It is possible to configure your container runtime to store images/containers on a separate filesystem.  Kubelet is now responsible for monitoring both the rootfs and the imagefs for disk pressure.  

Monitoring of disk pressure is done via EvictionHard settings.  If these settings are over the threshold, Kubelet will flag the node as having disk pressure.  By default, we include settings for imagefs.available.  

It is possible to override these settings on kubelet startup via EvictionHard and EvictionSoft settings.  

If one has a separate filesystem, or mounts a new disk to the default container location, then we are operating in a separate filesystem case.  

If a user does not specify EvictionHard/EvictionSoft settings, then we will not flag the node as having disk pressure if the image filesystem is above the threshold.

At a minimum, we should log a warning if the image filesystem is used but there are no imagefs.available or imagefs.inodesfree specified.  

### Why is this needed?

This can cause problems where the image filesystem is at capacity and we will still try to admit pods.

title: Image pull from private registry fails because of missing credentials
body:
### What happened?

When trying to pull a image from a private registry the request is executed without any kind of authorization.

The secret is manually created with
`kubectl create secret generic regcred --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=dc.json --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`

`dc.json` is a file like the following:
```json
{
    "auths": {
        "somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io": {
            "auth": "XYZ"
        }
    }
}
```
where XYZ is the base64 encoding of `:refresh_token` (there is no username as I want to dynamically get a token from a OAuth endpoint)

My pod is then specifying the `imagePullSecret` pointing to the `regcred` from above.

When creating the pod, after setting up a mitmproxy, I can see the following requests:
- HEAD to `https://somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io/v2/whateverimage/manifests/latest` which correctly fails with a 401 and returns a `Www-Authenticate` header set to `Bearer realm="https://somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io/oauth2/token",service="somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io",scope="repository:whateverimage:pull"`
- Then the request to the `/oauth2/token` endpoint is executed. The problem here is that it is executed as a GET (opposed to being a POST) and without the expected URLEncoded form including the refresh_token from the imagePullSecret.

Executing a `HTTPS_PROXY="127.0.0.1:8080" crictl pull --auth "XYZ"  somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io/whateverimage` gives me no issues and the image is pulled successfully.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the kubelet and the container runtime to properly talk to each other, but I am either doing something wrong or there is a bug 😄 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create an Azure Container Registry (or any image registry that is capable of OAuth AuthN)
- Setup a mitmproxy to watch the outgoing requests
- `kubectl create secret generic regcred --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=dc.json --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` where `dc.json` is a file like the following:  
  ```json
  {
      "auths": {
          "somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io": {
              "auth": "XYZ"
          }
      }
  }
  ```  
  (and XYZ is the base64 encoding of `:refresh_token`)
- Create a Pod referencing the imagePullSecret from above
- Check in mitmproxy there are 2 requests, one of the two should be a HEAD to `/v2/whateverimage/manifests/latest` and the other should be a POST (not a GET as above)
