title: Restrict addition of new e2e test images with a verify script
body:
We should check the images configured in test/e2e to ensure we're not adding new images:
 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/83e6636096548f4b49a94ece6bc4a26fd67e4449/test/utils/image/manifest.go#L229

In almost all cases, [test/images/agnhost](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/test/images/agnhost) should be extended to support any missing functionality and used as the sole image for new tests. This has been the policy in SIG Testing for at least a few years now.

To prevent regressing on this, we should check the list of images and permit tag updates but NOT adding any more names to the list.

We can do this with an allowlist against `e2e.test --list-images`

/sig testing
/kind test

Others are welcome to work on this, but I'll submit something soon if nobody beats me to it.
/assign

Follow up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122747, we should aim to ship something this release (1.30).

```

Upon reviewing the log, it appears that this issue arises when the `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure` condition transitions from True to False. Even if the current pressure is significant, but it will not immediately changing back to memory-pressure=True. As the documentation https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/#node-condition-oscillation, the default transition period is 5 minutes(eviction-pressure-transition-period default). It seems that this is leading to the accumulation of Pods in the ContainerStatusUnknown state 

In practical terms,  it appears that while `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure` condition transition from True to False should wait for a certain period, such as 5 minutes, but `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure` condition transition from False to True should not involve a waiting period and should occur immediately. this is will resolved the generation of many invalid Pods.



### What did you expect to happen?

some pod are in `ContainerStatusUnknown` state, but not a large numbers.

title: Feature request: reserving memory buffer for workload on a cluster node
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We would like to be able to reserve some amount of memory (`buffer`) for our workload on a cluster node. 
Scheduler should not over-subscribe a `New Allocatable` = [Allocatable](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/reserve-compute-resources/#node-allocatable) - `buffer`.
[Node-pressure eviction](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/) should still use an “old” `Allocatable` for evicting pods.

### Why is this needed?

This memory buffer would allow us to withstand memory consumption spikes and avoid OOMKilled errors.
This memory buffer would be available for any pod from our workload if this pod happens to temporarily need significantly more memory than configured in a memory request setting.
Such memory buffer would be especially helpful if [Memory QoS](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/11/26/qos-memory-resources/) feature gets enabled. 

We have very dynamic workload. We run a service which executes customer’s builds. For every new build our service creates a new pod that lives for a short time.
Memory consumption of such a pod can vary. In some cases it can try to consume significantly more memory than configured in a memory request setting of the pod.
If a node is fully packed with pods, it can lead to OOMKilled error and pod eviction.

We can only roughly guess possible memory consumption value because it depends on build type and build configuration provided by a customer.
Therefore, memory request settings which we configure cannot be precise.
Currently, we need to configure quite high memory request setting to minimize a likelihood of OOMKilled errors. 
This is very cost inefficient because we waste a lot memory on a node.

title: add opt-in compression support in storage factory
body:
### What would you like to be added?

add opt-in compression support in storage factory to give the capability to shrink the data size landing to storage. the default compression can be snappy, and other options can choose: zstd, zlib, etc. and it is also allowed to have customized compression registered.

### Why is this needed?

the data size keeps climbing along with time(e.g. 8~9 years). the performance of etcd degrades when DB size is too large(the promised db size from official site is 8GB), e.g. 16GB or larger. a compression can give a direct cure to shrink the data size to 30% with affordable CPU time.  lower or higher compression level can be used on demand.

### What did you expect to happen?

when kubelet restart, pod's postStart hook can always be run.

title: imagePullSecrets has no effect when registry prefix and location are different with cri-o
body:
### What happened?

I have a private registry with basic auth that mimics as another private registry to reduce code writing. The registry is a [docker distribution](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/) solution with proxy-mode for latter. Then i have **mirrors.conf** for cri-o as is:

When i execute
`crictl pull --creds admin:pass private.registry/image:tag`
everything is ok. But when i create a pod and a secret then i have this error with the pod:
`Failed to pull image "private.registry/image:tag": rpc error: code = Unknown desc = reading manifest tag in mirror.registry/image: unauthorized: authentication required`

If i rewrite **mirrors.conf** for cri-o when prefix and location are the same then no issues whatsoever. 

### What did you expect to happen?

When registry prefix and location are different then images should be pulled correctly with k8s secret.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**mirrors.conf** cri-o config for registries, when i have an error:
```
[[registry]]
prefix = private.registry
location = mirror.registry
```
**mirrors.conf** when everything works as expected:
```
[[registry]]
prefix = mirror.registry
location = mirror.registry**

```
pod manifest:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod
  namespace: my-ns
spec:
  containers:
    - image: private.registry/image:tag
      name: pod
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: registry-secret

```
secret manifest:
```
apiVersion: v1
data:
  .dockerconfigjson: base64-encoded-auths
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: registry-secret
  namespace: my-ns
type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson

```



### Anything else we need to know?

Both `crictl pull --creds` and `crictl pull auth` works as expected so i guess that cri-o works as intended.

title: Readiness probes are called even when pod is in terminating state
body:
### What happened?

When i deleted a pod using readiness probe saw below events

Events:
  Type     Reason     Age                 From     Message
  ----     ------     ----                ----     -------
  Normal   Killing    3m3s                kubelet  Stopping container xxxxxxx
  Warning  Unhealthy  35s (x10 over 14d)  kubelet  Readiness probe failed:


### What did you expect to happen?

Based on the issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/52817 and PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/98571 I expected readiness probe should not be called for a terminating pod similar to startup and liveness probe. Any specific reason we did not include readiness probe in this check.

	// Graceful shutdown of the pod.
	if w.pod.ObjectMeta.DeletionTimestamp != nil && (w.probeType == liveness || w.probeType == startup) {
		klog.V(3).Infof("Pod deletion requested, setting %v probe result to success: %v - %v",
			w.probeType.String(), format.Pod(w.pod), w.container.Name)
		if w.probeType == startup {
			klog.Warningf("Pod deletion requested before container has fully started: %v - %v",
				format.Pod(w.pod), w.container.Name)
		}
		// Set a last result to ensure quiet shutdown.
		w.resultsManager.Set(w.containerID, results.Success, w.pod)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod using readiness probe and a preStop hook so that deletion takes time. Delete the pod. You can still see readiness probe getting called for this pod.

title: Accessing NodePort on K8S host has latency when reaching Pods across different hosts
body:
### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster on Debian 12.4 operating system. I am using a test image, exposing a port to obtain the container's name. I use this method to determine which Pod the request is assigned to.

As shown in the screenshot below, accessing the Pod on the local machine works fine. However, if the request is assigned to a Pod on another host, there is a 1-second delay before receiving a response. Upon inspecting the packets using tcpdump, I observed that the first request resulted in a connection reset, and I am not quite sure about the cause of this issue.

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/104751498/d2fb1b0e-d2ea-4627-b691-9d6bfbc1398f)

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/104751498/84aa407e-4387-47fe-94f1-384950f0909a)

Deployed Kubernetes environment is functioning properly on CentOS 7.9 operating system.

title: [FR] Vertical Pod Autoscaling leveraging InPlacePodVerticalScaling
body:
### What would you like to be added?

As InPlacePodVerticalScaling has already been supported, I'd like a feature named VPA(Vertical Pod Autoscaling) which is similar to [Horizontal Pod Autoscaling](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/):
For the pod associated with a VPA, when the CPU resource(or other metric) reach a per-defined threshold, trigger InPlacePodVerticalScaling automatically.

### Why is this needed?

Current InPlacePodVerticalScaling can be only triggered manually. 
It can't be used in practical as human can't always monitor the pod status.
We need an automation solution to trigger InPlacePodVerticalScaling.

title: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
body:
### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue, or it could be a kube-proxy bug. Is it related to the following code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a07b1aaa5b39b351ec8586de800baa5715304a3f/pkg/proxy/metaproxier/meta_proxier.go#L55-L58
Additionally, I believe that in a dual-stack environment, if `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with one IP address range and the other IP address range is not configured, then the other IP address range cannot have all-zeros listening. Otherwise, the already configured IP address range may lose the non-all-zeros listening.


### What did you expect to happen?

In a dual-stack environment, if `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with one IP address range and the other IP address range is not configured, then the other IP address range cannot have all-zeros listening. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a dual-stack environment, `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with only one IP address range.Additionally, a Service with healthCheckNodePort is created.

title: sidecar container readniess result to be used in Pod ready state also for pod.spec.restartPolicy = Never or OnFailure
body:
### What happened?

I created a pod with sidecar container with following manifest:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: simple-webapp
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: "key1"
    operator: "Exists"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
  initContainers:
    - name: init-service
      image:  busybox
      command:
        - sleep
        - 5s
    - name: sidecar
      image:  busybox
      command:
        - sleep
        - 30s
      volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-logs
          mountPath: /var/log/nginx
      readinessProbe:
        exec:
          command:
          - cat
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 5
      imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
      restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: main-application
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
      - name: shared-logs
        mountPath: /var/log/nginx
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "100Mi"
        cpu: "0.5"
  volumes:
    - name: shared-logs
      emptyDir: {}
  restartPolicy: Never

```

watch the pod readiness. 
```
#before the sidecar container be restarted , the readiness is 2/2
watch kubectl  get pod
Every 2.0s: kubectl get pod                                                     

NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
simple-webapp           2/2     Running   0          36s

#after the sidecar container be restarted, the pod readiness is 1/2, sidecar readiness result is not be used to the pod. 
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
simple-webapp           1/2     Running   2          2m15s

```
in [Sidecar containers and Pod lifecycle](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/#sidecar-containers-and-pod-lifecycle), it's mentioned "If a readinessProbe is specified for this init container, its result will be used to determine the ready state of the Pod."

it's true only for pod.spec.restartPolicy = Always, sidecar container readniess result will be used in Pod ready state, neither "Never" or "OnFailure".

I tested with v1.29.0

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect "If a readinessProbe is specified for this init container, its result will be used to determine the ready state of the Pod." also applicable to  pod.spec.restartPolicy = "Never" or "OnFailure".

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: Topology spreading can become imbalanced during pod eviction
body:
### What happened?

We saw topology spreading constraints violated when a pod was evicted from a node and rescheduled on another node. In our deployment we want the 3 pods to be distributed in 3 availability zones but we saw 0/1/2 distributions multiple times. 

When a node is drained it evicts all pods on it and k8s schedules new pods on other nodes to satisfy deployment's replicas spec. In our environment, when this event happens the newly scheduled pod is always created at least 10 seconds before the corresponding old pod is terminated. When scheduling the new pod k8s sees evenly distributed pods without knowing a pod will be terminated soon, so it schedules pod to an arbitrary domain which is sometimes different from the domain in which the old pod is running. 

This is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105661 but it happens during node draining so the new and old pods are in the same replica, which means we can't use the `MatchLabelKeys` to distinguish the old an new pods. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I am not sure this is a bug or limitation of topology spreading constraints. If it is a limitation please document this limitation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy a 3 replica service to a k8s cluster running in 3 AZ region with the following topologySpreadConstraints

```
topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.k8s.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
```

Drain the node in one zone and check the pods distribution after

title: [Proposal]  Add most non-deprecated flags to the Kubelet configuration API
body:
**Proposal:** Add most non-deprecated flags to the Kubelet configuration API. These will still be settable via flag (flag values override config values).

**Background:**
The decision of which Kubelet flags to expose in the Kubelet configuration was historically tied to the Dynamic Kubelet Configuration feature. Specifically, the configuration was designed to be shared across nodes. Dynamic Kubelet Configuration has since been deprecated and removed, and this concern is no longer relevant

**Motivation:**
Consolidating more of the configuration into the configuration API will let users manage their Kubelet configuration via a single API surface, rather than needing to split the configuration across flags and a configuration file.

**Add:**

- [ ] HostnameOverride 
- [ ] NodeIP
- [ ] config.ContainerRuntimeOptions (except deprecated PodSandboxImage)
- [ ] RuntimeCgroups
- [ ] ImageCredentialProviderConfigFile
- [ ] ImageCredentialProviderBinDir
- [ ] CertDirectory 
- [ ] RootDirectory 
- [ ] WindowsService 
- [ ] WindowsPriorityClass 
- [ ] CloudProvider - note: this may turn into a boolean option

**Open Question: "alpha" flags**
These flags claim to be alpha (`<Warning: Alpha feature>`), but appear to be ungated. These should probably be treated as default-GA, and added to the config.

- [ ] NodeLabels
- [ ] LockFilePath
- [ ] ExitOnLockContention

**The following options will remain flag only:**

- KubeConfig, BootstrapKubeConfig - We could consider adding these, but it seems odd to point one config file at the other.
- KubeletConfigFile, KubeletDropinConfigDirectory - Point to the Kubelet config (don't want a circular reference!)
- Deprecated flags:
    - MinimumGCAge
    - MaxPerPodContainerCount
    - MaxContainerCount
    - RegisterSchedulable
    - KeepTerminatedPodVolumes
    - ExperimentalMounterPath
    - ExperimentalNodeAllocatableIgnoreEvictionThreshold
    - CloudConfigFile
    - PodSandboxImage
    - `azure-container-registry-config`
- cAdvisor flags - Accidental flag leak
- version flag / help flag - Not config
- logging flags - Relevant fields are already included in the logging configuration

**Historical References:**
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/40117 - Flags that can't be shared across nodes are moved out of shared config type (removed Hostname, NodeIP)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/44061 - Extract CROptions from KubeletConfig
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/46254 - Removed CertDirectory, RootDirectory, CloudProvider

/sig node
/milestone v1.30
/kind cleanup api-change

title: validatingadmissionpolicystatus reports error when using spec.variables
body:
### What happened?

When I load a policy definition like this

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: loadbalancer.servicenow.net
spec:
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiVersions: ["v1"]
      apiGroups:   [""]
      resources:   ["services"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
  matchConditions:
  - name: "only-loadbalancer-services"
    expression: object.spec.type == "LoadBalancer"
  paramKind:
    apiVersion: control.servicenow.net/v1beta1
    kind: TenantPermission
  variables:
  - name: loadbalancerid
    expression: "'ccm.snowsk8s.servicenow.net/lb-service-id' in object.metadata.annotations ? object.metadata.annotations['ccm.snowsk8s.servicenow.net/lb-service-id'] : 'none'"
  validations:
    - expression: variables.loadbalancerid in params.permissions.loadbalancerid
      reason: Forbidden
      messageExpression: "'Namespace ' + string(namespaceObject.metadata.name) + ' does not have permissions to loadbalancer ' + string(variables.loadbalancerid)"
  failurePolicy: Fail
```


The object is updated with the following status
```yaml
status:
  observedGeneration: 2
  typeChecking:
    expressionWarnings:
    - fieldRef: spec.validations[0].expression
      warning: |
        /v1, Kind=Service: ERROR: <input>:1:1: undeclared reference to 'variables' (in container '')
         | variables.loadbalancerid in params.permissions.loadbalancerid
         | ^
    - fieldRef: spec.validations[0].messageExpression
      warning: |
        /v1, Kind=Service: ERROR: <input>:1:111: undeclared reference to 'variables' (in container '')
         | 'Namespace ' + string(namespaceObject.metadata.name) + ' does not have permissions to loadbalancer ' + string(variables.loadbalancerid)
         | ..............................................................................................................^
```

While this error is reported, the policy does seem to be fully functioning

```
// Try to claim someone elses loadbalancer in the a different namespace
k apply -f testing/someones-loadbalancer.yaml   
Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "testing/someones-loadbalancer.yaml": services "idonthavealoadbalancer" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'loadbalancer.servicenow.net' with binding 'deny-non-owning-loadbalancer' denied request: Namespace workload1 does not have permissions to loadbalancer 123someoneelses123

// Try to claim a loadbalancer without any valid ID
 k apply -f testing/idonthavemyown.yaml
Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "testing/idonthavemyown.yaml": services "soneone-elses-loadbalancer" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'loadbalancer.servicenow.net' with binding 'deny-non-owning-loadbalancer' denied request: Namespace workload1 does not have permissions to loadbalancer none

// A valid request
k apply -f testing/my-loadbalancer.yaml 
service/my-loadbalancer configured
```

This is similar to the documented examples
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/validating-admission-policy/#variable-composition

### What did you expect to happen?

No error reported on a valid spec

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a a policy that uses variables
Observe the status of the newly created policy

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Scheduler:  Share `frameworkImpl.waitingPods` among profiles
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I hope to share the `waitingPods` among multiple profiles, instead of creating a new `waitingPods` in each profiles with the current implementation.

In other words, `waitingPods` is only instantiated once in a scheduler app.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a1ffdedf782edf1472102b0b99c1467d4ed39753/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L253-L258


@Huang-Wei @ahg-g  PTAL, Is there any negative impact of this change that I didn't consider, thanks.

### Why is this needed?

In some scenarios, I need to traverse `all pods` waiting in the permit stage within the current scheduler app, rather than the pods that using the current profile for scheduling and waiting in the permit stage.

For example, we want use [coscheduling](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins/blob/master/pkg/coscheduling/README.md) to achieve `all-or-nothing`. And we have abstracted the concept of a `Cluster`, where there are two deployments under each cluster. Each deployments use different scheduler profile, and one cluster corresponds to one podGroup, as following:
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/18323315/256ffd20-6adc-4dc5-b249-d6ffcafed303)

Then, we want pods in one cluster (podA1, podA2, podB1) to be scheduled succeed/failed together. 

We assume that all pods can pass through the filter plugins, and `podA2` is the last to be scheduled. At this point, `podA1` and `podB1` are both waiting in the permit stage. Afterwards, we traverse the `waitingPods` to complete the permit waiting for `podA1` and `podB1`. However, from an implementation perspective, now we can only see `podA1` in `waitingPods`, `podB1` cannot be seen, because`podA2` & `podB1` use different scheduling profiles. Which will cause `podB1` timeout during the permit phase, even if all pods within the podGroup are successfully scheduled.

title: Kubelet - failed to initialize top level QOS containers: root container [kubepods] doesn't exist
body:
### What happened?

Starting the kubelet the first time after a system reboot,  the kubelet fails with:
`E0125 00:20:56.003890    2172 kubelet.go:1466] "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="failed to initialize top level QOS containers: root container [kubepods] doesn't exist"`

Which, sort of is a lie.   The root cause is actually that `cpuset` does not exist in `/sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control` 

After the kubelet exits, systemd restarts in,  and then all is fine after that,  until the next time the OS is restarted.  

I tried to track it down,  create.go does add the cpuset to `cgroup.subtree_control`,  and it remains there until `common.go:setUnitProperties()` is executed,  at which time `cpuset` appears to be disabled and disappears.  The other controllers are unaffected.   On the subsequent kubelet restart, `cpuset` does get added again,  and remains after the call to setUnitProperties().   

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the kubelet to start and not exit on all starts of the kubelet. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The OS I am using is RHEL 9 on s390x.   
1) Boot the OS
2) Start the kubelet (I start with `kubeadm init` or `kubeadm join`.
3) Observer the kubelet starts,  fails, and then restarts.   Subsequent restarts of the kubelet are successful until the OS rebooted. (Likely due to after a reboot, the /sys/fs/cgroups is fresh,  unlike subsequent restarts of the kubelet)

title: Publish finer-grained failure reason for podFailurePolicy
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When a Job failure is triggered via PodFailurePolicy, we currently set a generic reason on the failure condition, which is "PodFailurePolicy"

It would be great if the reason is more specific about the failure reason, which exact rule failed the job. There are few ways of doing that: 

1) Add a `Reason` field to `PodFailurePolicyRule` to allow users to _optionally_ decide what reason should show up on the condition when the rule is triggered. We verify that it should be a single word with a specific length limit (because reasons are typically machine readable codes).

2) In the case of onExitCodes to have the code appended to the reason, like "PodFailurePolicy-ExitCode143". But this will be tricky to do for the OnPodConditions case.

My preference is the first option.



### Why is this needed?

This will give higher order APIs that use Job as a building block (such as JobSet) control in how they react to the child Job failure based on the container exit code. See https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/pull/381 for more details.


/wg batch
/sig apps

I've provided a stripped down Job manifest as follows.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:

  namespace: default 
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: container-notready
          image: busybox:latest
          command: ["/bin/sh"]
          args: ["-c", "sleep 180 && exit 1"]
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
  backoffLimit: 1
```

The first time the container starts up there is no readiness probe. On container restart, we **should not** check for readiness.

title: configure topologySpreadConstraints in order to ignore zones which have no health nodes?
body:
**How can we configure topologySpreadConstraints in order to ignore zones which have no health nodes?**


**Details**
We prepared nodes (kubernetes.io/hostname) and zones (topology.kubernetes.io/zone) as follows.
```
Zone: E01
node1
node2
node3

Zone: E02
node4

Zone: E03
node5
```
Then we deployed the following deployment.
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dummy
  labels:
    app: test
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: dummy
        image: nginx
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: test
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                - key: app
                  operator: In
                  values:
                  - test
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
```
4 Pods were spreaded as follows.

```
# Zone: E01
node1   Pod
node2
node3   Pod

# Zone: E02
node4   Pod

# Zone: E03
node5   Pod

$ kubectl get pod -o wide
NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP             NODE    READINESS GATES
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-dmhvr   1/1     Running   0          8s    10.130.2.20    node1   <none>

dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-xkbkb   1/1     Running   0          8s    10.131.0.56    node5   <none>

```
Then I powered off node4.
We had expected that the pod running on node4 would be moved to node5 of Zone: E03, since we set topologySpreadConstraints with "maxSkew: 1", "topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone" and "whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule".
But in actual result, the new pod got stacked with pending state.
```
$ kubectl get pod -o wide
NAME                     READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE     IP             NODE    READINESS GATES
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-dmhvr   1/1     Running       0          8m50s   10.130.2.20    node1   <none>
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-m22hq   1/1     Terminating   0          8m50s   10.128.5.158   node4   <none>
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-nrk8z   1/1     Running       0          8m50s   10.129.2.103   node3   <none>
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-xgs68   0/1     Pending       0          83s     <none>         <none>  <none>
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-xkbkb   1/1     Running       0          8m50s   10.131.0.56    node5   <none>
```
The pending Pod started to be scheduled on node5 after we unlabeled Zone: E02 from node4.

```
$ kubectl label node example-cluster-node topology.kubernetes.io/zone-
node/example-cluster-node unlabeled

$ kubectl get pod -o wide
NAME                     READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE   IP             NODE    READINESS GATES
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-dmhvr   1/1     Running       0          31m   10.130.2.20    node1   <none>
dummy-XXXXXXXXXX-m22hq   1/1     Terminating   0          31m   10.128.5.158   node4   <none>

My expectation was that topologySpreadConstraints ignores E02 and schedule a new pod on node5.

Maybe should we use nodeTaintsPolicy?

Can we do it by setting nodeTaintsPolicy?

title: Kubernetes Node Resources may not have provider ID populated when using external cloud provider
body:
### What happened?

When using an external/out of band cloud providers, the responsibility of adding the provider ID to a Node resource moves from kubelet to the node controller. However because of this change, kubelet will create a node without the provider ID specified and may mark the node as ready. This has become an issue in GKE where workloads are scheduled on the node, but external networking (Ingress and Gateway) cannot proceed because the providerID is missing leading to possible downtimes every time a new node is created.

Another consequence is that if populating the [provider ID fails for any reason](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ae185414f4e94e969399c40b23995af6f85fa37f/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L434-L437), the Node object is never updated which means information such as the zone topology and provider ID don't exist. EPS Controller uses the zone topology to populate the EPS.

### What did you expect to happen?

When using an external cloud provider, I would expect that the provider ID should gate whether the Node is considered ready or not. This would ensure that workloads are not scheduled on to a Node, until it has all relevant information populated.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On any cluster that uses an external cloud provider, there will be two API calls made when a new node is created. A create call from kubelet where provider ID isn't populated and an update by the node controller.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Readiness probe success during preStop hook causes replicas scaling
body:
### What happened?

We are using Readiness and liveness probes in the deployment while `preStop` hook is set to `sleep 60` in order to gracefully shutdown pods.

When we update a deployment by setting a new image, a new Pod is created.  Due to slow start of the JVM, it accidentally failed all initial Readiness and liveness probes attempts. Then the preStop hook is called and the pod is scheduled to be killed after a period of time (for example 60 seconds in our case).

According to the current design, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122824#issuecomment-1896099927, the Readiness probe will not be stopped. And in some cases, we've observed the Readiness probe passed and the new RS was scaled up while the old RS was scaled down.

But this Pod will be terminated after 60 seconds. So after some time, no Pod is healthy.

### What did you expect to happen?

The Readiness probe does not lead to the reconcile of deployment-controller.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The timeline is designed as following,

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/2568208/65a55d67-a169-48ec-a5c3-778be0771350)

Any readiness probe attempt pass within the orange zone will cause this issue.

First, we can start a Kubernetes version `1.22` with kind,

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
  image: kindest/node:v1.22.17@sha256:f5b2e5698c6c9d6d0adc419c0deae21a425c07d81bbf3b6a6834042f25d4fba2
```

Then write a simple Go application to control when the probes can pass,

```go
package main

import (
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"time"
)

var (
	_                      http.Handler = (*healthHandler)(nil)
	startTime                           = time.Now()
	healthThresholdSeconds int
)

type healthHandler struct{}

func (h healthHandler) ServeHTTP(writer http.ResponseWriter, request *http.Request) {
	if time.Now().Sub(startTime).Seconds() > float64(healthThresholdSeconds) {
		writer.WriteHeader(200)
		writer.Write([]byte("ok"))
		return
	}
	writer.WriteHeader(500)
	writer.Write([]byte("not healthy"))
}

func main() {
	flag.IntVar(&healthThresholdSeconds, "health-threshold-seconds", 30, "delay")
	flag.Parse()
	log.Println(fmt.Sprintf("health probe will start after %d seconds", healthThresholdSeconds))
	log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", &healthHandler{}))
}
```

Then deploy this application to the cluster,

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 0
    type: RollingUpdate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: kubernetes-prober:latest
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: "64Mi"
              cpu: "10m"
          args:
            - -health-threshold-seconds=55
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command:
                  - sleep
                  - "30"
          livenessProbe:
            failureThreshold: 3
            httpGet:
              path: /check
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
            successThreshold: 1
            timeoutSeconds: 5
          readinessProbe:
            failureThreshold: 3
            httpGet:
              path: /check
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
            successThreshold: 1
            timeoutSeconds: 5
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Startup Probe does help in this scenario if we patch the deployment above,

```yaml
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /check
              port: 8080
            failureThreshold: 60
            periodSeconds: 5
```

1.27.x also suffers from this issue,

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
  image: kindest/node:v1.22.17@sha256:f5b2e5698c6c9d6d0adc419c0deae21a425c07d81bbf3b6a6834042f25d4fba2
```

title: Duplicate OwnerReferences Can Deny Service To SSA Clients
body:
### What happened?

When some actor manages to add duplicate `OwnerReferences` to an object, any other client attempting to use server-side apply to mutate the object will fail client-side.

Consider some `Service`:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2020-07-10T22:57:31Z"
  name: service-name
  namespace: service-namespace
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: group.whatever.com/v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: false
    controller: false
    kind: SomeKind
    name: someName
    uid: 1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e
  - apiVersion: group.whatever.com/v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: false
    controller: false
    kind: SomeKind
    name: someName
    uid: 1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e
  resourceVersion: "304470743"
  uid: 8cf44d74-d698-450f-abb6-b52f3511a85b
spec:
  clusterIP: 172.30.249.81
  clusterIPs:
  - 172.30.249.81
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  ipFamilies:
  - IPv4
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ports:
  - port: 443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 5443
  selector:
    app: whatever
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

When a client attempts to send a server-side apply PATCH, client-side validation fails:

```
E0131 12:33:54.677801       1 queueinformer_operator.go:319] sync {"update" "service-namespace/service-name"} failed: failed to create manager for existing fields: failed to convert new object (service-namespace/service-name; /v1, Kind=Service) to smd typed: errors:
  .metadata.ownerReferences: duplicate entries for key [uid="1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e"]
  .metadata.ownerReferences: duplicate entries for key [uid="1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e"]
```

### What did you expect to happen?

If unique `OwnerReferences` is an invariant required of objects, perhaps we can add some ratcheting validation for objects in `etcd` that enforces it. I can't see a good reason any client would want duplicate entries, but we must have uniqueness for SSA to function here.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a resource with a duplicate `OwnerReference` - don't use `kubectl edit` as that client will helpfully dedupe things for you. Then try using SSA.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

--- a/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go
+++ b/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go
@@ -19,6 +19,7 @@ package pleg
 import (
        "context"
        "fmt"

        "sync"
        "sync/atomic"
        "time"
@@ -176,7 +177,7 @@ func (g *GenericPLEG) Healthy() (bool, error) {

title: APIServer watchcache lost events
body:
### What happened?

It appears that APIServer watchcache occasionally lost events. We can confirm that this is NOT a stale watchcache issue.

In some 1.27 clusters, we observed that both watchcache in 2 APIServer instances are pretty up-to-date (object created within 60s can be found from both cache). However, we believe some delete events were lost in the APIServer watchcache. In the bad apiserver, a few objects that deleted more than 24 hours ago still shows up in one of the APIServer cache. It's possible that other types of events (e.g. update) may also get lost, but they are not as noticeable as delete event since it can recover from the 2nd update event even if the first update event is lost.

This issue impacts k8s clients that use an informer cache. Once the informer get the same events from the bad APIServer, it won't recover until it gets restarted. Replacing the bad APIServer with a good one won't help the informer to discover the missing events.

We have observed at least 6 clusters run into this issue in EKS. 5 of them started to have this issue shortly after control plane upgrade but 1 cluster started to have this issue more than 1 hour before the control plane upgrade kicked in.

The clusters were running OK on 1.26, the issue started to show up when the clusters were upgraded to 1.27.

We saw `apiserver_watch_cache_events_received_total{resource="pods"}` diverged between the 2 apiserver instances. during the incident while the delta between the 2 apiserver instances are expected to be the same.

We run the following command `kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/my-ns/pods/my-pod?resourceVersion=0"` on 2 different APIServers. One returns an object and the other returns NotFound.

EDIT: add some additional data points.
We did see the etcd memory kept increasing during the incident.

We believe the components that triggered this is Falco v0.35.1. It is a daemonset and it made a lot of watch requests w/o resourceVersion. All 6 clusters have a couple hundreds of nodes when the incident started. 

In my repro cluster, I saw one etcd has much higher `etcd_debugging_mvcc_pending_events_total`(over 1 million) than the other etcd instances (< 20k).

### What did you expect to happen?

APIServer watch cache not to lose event.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

EDIT:
We have a way to repro in EKS. It may not be the minimum steps to repro.
- Create a 1.27 cluster with 800 worker nodes
- Maintain high pod churn in the cluster. I have 1000 per minute
- Deploy falco using helm: `helm install falco falcosecurity/falco --create-namespace --namespace falco --version 3.6.0 --values falco-chart-values.yaml` Note chart version 3.6.0 has falco version 0.35.1. You need to mirror the falco images to your container registry. Otherwise, your kubelet will be throttled by docker hub heavily and it will cause daemonset pods to come up slowly.

<details>

<summary>
falco-chart-values.yaml
</summary>

```yaml
json_output: true
log_syslog: false
collectors:
  containerd:
    enabled: false
  crio:
    enabled: false
  docker:
    enabled: false
driver:
  enabled: true

  loader:
    enabled: true
    initContainer:
      image:
        registry: your-account.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com
        repository: david-falco-driver-loader
        tag: 0.35.1
        pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
image:
  registry: your-account.dkr.ecr.us-west-2.amazonaws.com
  repository: david-falco
  tag: 0.35.1
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
podPriorityClassName: system-node-critical

    tag: 0.5.1

title: apiserver OOM due to terminate all watchers for a specified crd cacher
body:
### What happened?

when crd spec changes, all watchers connected to the cacher of the crd will be terminated. this will result to informer watch from last RV again. the last RV is almost always less than the global RV after cacher recreated, so a "too old resource version" error is returned by cacher and informer will do relist operation which may result to kube-apiserver OOM.

### What did you expect to happen?

- send latest rv to watchers before terminate it
- graceful terminate watchers when to recreate cache just like when to shutdown apiserver to avoid any thundering herd issues.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- create a crd and create some cr resources
- update crd spec
- then there will be some relist request

body:
### What happened?

See context in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122721 and we disabeld it in presubmit and periodic CIs. 

> We discussed this in sig-node today. We are temporarily going to not block on these failures to unblock the current release but will target fixing this issue as a priority before the next minor release.

Discussion context about this bug in slack is https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1706638623162379?thread_ts=1706055745.168469&cid=C0BP8PW9G with @mrunalp and @dchen1107.

Static Pods should be started normally when EventedPLEG is enabled.
- revert to alpha due to this bug: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122697

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It is observed in alpha CIs like #122721.

### Anything else we need to know?

EventedPLEG has a known issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121349, and it will cause static pod startup failure(most time)

title: PostStartHook "scheduling/bootstrap-system-priority-classes" failed: unable to add default system priority classes: timed out waiting for the condition`
body:
### What happened?

PostStartHook failed
`E0122 06:54:22.018964      10 writers.go:131] apiserver was unable to write a fallback JSON response: http: Handler timeout
W0122 06:54:22.457480      10 storage_scheduling.go:106] unable to get PriorityClass system-node-critical: Get "https://*.*.*.*:8443/apis/scheduling.k8s.io/v1/priorityclasses/system-node-critical": net/http: TLS handshake timeout. Retrying...
F0122 06:54:22.457615      10 hooks.go:203] PostStartHook "scheduling/bootstrap-system-priority-classes" failed: unable to add default system priority classes: timed out waiting for the condition`


### What did you expect to happen?

PostStartHook not failed

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.Apiserver is deployed using static Pods
2.The other service accesses Apiserver through Apiserver's serviceip
3.Limit the CPU of the Apiserver as much as possible
4.Simulate as many requests as possible to overload Apiserver's CPU

### Anything else we need to know?

All Poststarthooks are called asynchronously by the go coroutine
Through reading the code, I found that the service and endpoint tuning process of Apiserver is also carried out by goroutine(pkg/controlplane/instance.go:508:)
his leads to the problem of executing other poststarthooks after the Apiserver has been placed on the endpoint back end to provide service. Since Apiserver has already provided services at this time, if there is a high concurrency and many requests, the load of Apiserver will be too high, and eventually the PostStartHook request will time out, and Apiserver will eventually kill itself

title: Fake client does not populate watch with initial state
Pod looses network connection (connection reset errors) during preStop period
body:
### What happened? **Environment:** I am running an Spring boot HTTP server and an HTTP client pod, where the client sends requests to the server using the `myserver.svc.cluster.local` address. Both server and client communicate over a keep-alive session. And the server is configured with a `preStop` hook set to 10 seconds during rolling updates ``` A(pod)--- | -- myserver(svc) <--[HTTP request with keep-alive]-- myclient(svc) --- C(pod) B(pod)--- ``` **Issue:** When performing a rolling update on the `myserver`, the client experiences a 2 times of a connection reset error. Each connection reset error occurs immediately as the each server pod enter the Terminating state. (beginning of preStop session)
**Detailed condition:** Despite the preStop being set to 10 seconds, which should theoretically allow existing keep-alive sessions to continue without accepting new HTTP traffic, the server's IP is immediately removed from the endpoints upon the preStop hook initiation. As a result, keep-alive sessions, which should have been maintained with Pod A, are transferred to Pod B. **ex)** For example, the client sends an HTTP GET request with a sequence number `61293`, which was associated with a keep-alive session on Pod A. However, as soon as preStop on Pod A initiates, this packet is redirected to Pod B. Pod B, receiving a packet with an unexpected sequence number, sends an RST packet back to the client, resulting in a connection reset error. ### What did you expect to happen? While I expect that new HTTP traffic will not reach the pod during the preStop period, **I also expect that existing keep-alive sessions should be preserved.** However, this is not happening. Is this a bug, or is it intended behavior? ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? . ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version

title: GetDeviceBindMountRefs not effective
body:
### What happened?

Even if multiple block device files exist in `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/<pv-name>/dev/`, `GetDeviceBindMountRefs` returns nil.

### What did you expect to happen?

It returns what are present in that directory

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Hard to reproduce. But with a simple Go program, we can see the error:
```go
func main() {
	entries, err := os.ReadDir(os.Args[1])
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, entry := range entries {
		println(entry.Name(), entry.Type())
	}
}
```
Run this with `./main /var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/*/dev/`. It outputs:
```
364c407c-5603-4338-9e86-fc8e5a3c5153 0
ceebc348-9906-4d2c-a730-07d56f6105c5 0
```

### Anything else we need to know?

`os.ReadDir` reads the directory in the system filesystem (maybe ext4), which does not know the mounted block device file (in devtmpfs) over it. So, it always returns the information about the hidden regular file.

However, I suspect we may have possible leakage here. We may need to check carefully for leakage before fixing this. Or we will break existing setup. Specifically, we write 5 global states when a CSI volumeDevice is in use.

1. `/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/staging/<pv>/<pv>`
2. `/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/publish/<pv>/<pod uid>`
3. `/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/<pv>/dev/<pod uid>`
4. `/pods/<pod uid>/volumeDevices/kubernetes.io~csi/<pv>`    symlink to 2
5. loop device

`GetDeviceBindMountRefs` checks for 3, volume reconstruction after kubelet restart checks for 4. Then 1-3 may leak and `GetDeviceBindMountRefs` may fail if 1-3 success but 4 does not.

title: K8s can't live without a default route
body:
### What happened?

Derived from https://github.com/projectcalico/calico/issues/8481

I use a virtual cluster with router VMs. When I start without any router VM, no default route is setup on the K8s nodes. This makes load-balancing to services to fail, at least with proxy-mode=iptables/nftables, and just about all CNI-plugins to fail. In short, the cluster is dead.

With proxy-mode=ipvs service routing works, but there are more subtle problems, e.g. Calico doesn't start. I haven't investigated further.

### What did you expect to happen?

Well, to me it seems OK to _require_ a default route, but the problem must be documented somewhere where cluster admins will see it.

I can't really see any use-case where a default route is not set. Maybe when K8s is only used for SW-management, or security reasons.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a test cluster:
1. curl -k https://kluster-svc-address
2. ip ro delete default
3. curl -k https://kluster-svc-address

For instance on KinD:
```
root@default-control-plane:/# curl -k https://10.96.0.1
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:anonymous\" cannot get path \"/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}root@default-control-plane:/# ip ro del default
root@default-control-plane:/# curl -k https://10.96.0.1
curl: (7) Couldn't connect to server
root@default-control-plane:/# 
```


### Anything else we need to know?

IMO this is a documentation issue.

title: Is Graceful Node Shutdown enabled by default on a K8S cluster?
body:
### What happened?

As checked on the K8S documentation, the GracefulNodeShutdown was enabled by default in K8S 1.21 as beta: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/04/21/graceful-node-shutdown-beta/

But there is no update on this yet. I don't think this is GA yet.

### What did you expect to happen?

For a fresh EKS cluster created 1.25 (sufficiently after 1.21), I was expecting that it should have the GracefulNodeShutdown enabled. Hence, the systemd-inhibit --list should show kubelet.

title: Declarative field deprecation & deprecated field usage tracking
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I'd like a mechanism to denote that a field is deprecated in CRDs (as well as core/built-in types) and be able to track deprecated field usage via similar mechanisms to how we track deprecated API version usage.

Ideally, this would be an extra field in the AuditEvent structure, similar to:

```
deprecatedFieldUsages:
- spec.myDeprecatedField
```

Depending on how markers for deprecated fields are implemented, we *may* be able to include some kind of details on what version a field was deprecated (or possibly even removed) but I'd leave that TBD after further discussion with sig-apimachinery.

### Why is this needed?

As Kubernetes and third-party CRDs evolve, fields may be deprecated and (depending on the policies of the projects authoring these CRDs) may even be removed at a future date.

Currently, the only way to do this would be with a validating/mutating webhook of some sort, that could inspect the request body in POST/PUT requests and emit audit annotations.

By supporting this as a native feature, it'll ease platform operators managing upgrades and migrations of both Kubernetes and related ecosystem tools that utilise CRDs.

/sig apimachinery

title: Change encryption config reload success/failure metrics
body:
Change encryption config controller reload metrics to be consistent with other places (Authn, Authz)
xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4456/files#r1480546416

Combine `apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reload_failures_total` and `apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reload_success_total` into a single metric `apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reloads_total` with `status` with an enum value of `success` and `failure`.

/sig auth
/triage accepted

title: Parallel pod deletion makes kubectl stuck forever
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl delete pod` may become stuck during execution of the following steps:
* Restart kubelet `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Force remove all containers for static pods `crictl ps --name '(kube-apiserver|kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager|etcd)' -q | xargs -I CONTAINER sudo crictl rm -f CONTAINER`
* Try to delete some static pod `kubectl delete pod -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-k8s-control-plane-1`

Result: kubectl prints that the pod is deleted, but never exits.

It seems that the problem is caused by parallel deletion of the pod by kubelet.
Please see details in the steps to reproduce.


### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl exits.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install single-node cluster
2. Run script
<details>

```sh
#!/bin/bash

for i in {1..100} ; do
  echo "Attempt $i"
  systemctl restart kubelet
  crictl ps --name '(kube-apiserver|kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager|etcd)' -q | xargs -I CONTAINER sudo crictl rm -f CONTAINER
  for component in kube-apiserver kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager etcd; do
    while true ; do
      echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S,%N') delete $component"
      if kubectl --v=10 delete pod -n kube-system ${component}-k8s-control-plane-1 2> failed.txt ; then
        break
      fi
    done
  done
  for component in kube-apiserver kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager etcd; do
    while true ; do
      echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S,%N') get $component"
      if kubectl get pod -n kube-system ${component}-k8s-control-plane-1 | grep '1/1' ; then
        break
      fi
      sleep 5
    done
  done
done
```
</details>

title: Dynamic node lease renew interval
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make the node lease renew internal dynamic. For example, with default settings of `nodeLeaseDurationSeconds` being 40s, the node lease is renewed every 1/4 of `nodeLeaseDurationSeconds` (i.e. 10s). With this feature, it can be 20s, but if the renew is unsuccessful, the interval decreases to 10s and if it fails again, interval decreases to 5s. However, after 3 attempts, the interval resets to 20s.

### Why is this needed?

With increasing popularity in using k8s with a large number of nodes, it becomes a significant overhead for apiserver to just handle the node lease renew requests. As mentioned above, each node renews its lease every 10s so every node contributes 0.1 QPS just with lease renewing alone. Also worth mentioning, lease renew has to hit ETCD as it's a modification request, which is more expensive than cache read request (about 8ms vs 1ms under no stress). 

It's difficult to measure how much resource a lease renewing would cost and it's even more difficult taking extra overhead when under stress (and therefore perf degradation) into consideration but with this feature, we can potentially cut the request volume in half (i.e. 50% decrease) while minimize the risk of having fewer attempts for failed renew requests within `nodeLeaseDurationSeconds`. From non-audited observations, I expect 0.2 cores saved in a cluster of 200 nodes.

title: Implement `apiserver_watch_cache_read_wait` metric
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Part of https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2340

From https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/2340-Consistent-reads-from-cache/README.md#what-if-the-watch-cache-is-stale 


> Metric apiserver_watch_cache_read_wait will measure wait time experienced by reads for watch cache to become fresh. If user notices a latency request in they can use this metric to confirm that the issue is caused by watch cache.

For now posted as a "help wanted" issue, however if we cannot hit the timeline for 1.30 code freeze ([5th March](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-release/tree/master/releases/release-1.30#summary)) I would take it over so we don't miss. Still issue is simple enough that it can be quickly implemented.

Implementation tips:
* Add a metric around waitUnitlFreshAndBlock method https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f07b47c3d1e596f53640285afb0d53a81fe6f259/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L441
* Metric should be a histogram with latency buckets similar to api latency

title: Implement per-request watch cache opt-out
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Part of https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2340

From https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/2340-Consistent-reads-from-cache/README.md#what-if-the-watch-cache-is-stale 

> Per request override should allow user to compare request results without impacting other requests or requiring to redeploy whole cluster. The exact details of override API will be clarified during API review. In healthy situation, using this override should not cause any impact on the response, however it might increase resource usage. In our tests cpu load could increase tenfold. To prevent abuse access to it should be limited to users with `cluster-admin` role, rejecting the request otherwise.

This issue will require designing an API and going through API review. Definitely not a beginner issue

Up to now we have discussed using HTTP headers or adding another option for ListOptions struct. Some of my thoughts:
* Don't want to commit to stable API, as we don't want to design a full request debugging API. 
* It changes how requests are internally handled, but not API semantics. It doesn't make sense to be part of ListOptions that is passed to both watch cache and storage.
* On the other hand we want to avoid a obscure flag that make API surface hard to track.
* Should be included in API request cost calculations




### Why is this needed?

A way to debug watch cache

title: Implement checking etcd version to warn about deprecated etcd versions
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Part of https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2340

From https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/2340-Consistent-reads-from-cache/README.md#bug-in-etcd-progress-notification

> Only recently community discovered a bug https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15220 for requesting progress notification. This bug causes a race between sending an event and progress notification with the same revision. Normally we would expect to event to always come first, however due to the bug, progress notification might be sent first. Serving a consistent lists in that situation could result in returning too early and missing the event. The bug was only fixed in v3.4.25 and v3.5.8 (both 9 months old), which is too fresh for Kubernetes to not handle.
> 
> Our tests have shown that with the bug manual progress notification cannot be trusted at all. It causes a silent corruption that cannot be automatically detected prior to acting upon the corrupted data. For Beta, we propose to conditionally enable the feature in a way that mitigates the risk of unaware users stumbling on the bug.
> 
> We propose to implement a safeguard that will prevent enabling ConsistentListFromCache on etcd version with broken progress notification. During kube-apiserver startup we will verify etcd version by calling Status method and checking etcd patch version. The condition will only pass if all etcd endpoints have etcd version that includes the fix for https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15220.
> 
> The proposed behavior of the safeguard for Beta:
> 
> etcd version could not be acquired or etcd new enough - warn, but continue with whatever the current value of the feature gate is
> * etcd too old, feature gate not explicitly specified - warn and disable the feature
> * etcd too old, feature gate explicitly enabled - abort
> * etcd new enough - use whatever the current value of the feature gate is
>
> The proposed behavior of the safeguard for GA (feature gate locked to true):
> * etcd version could not be acquired - warn, but continue with the feature enabled
> * etcd too old - abort
> * etcd new enough - enable feature
> 
> Checking etcd version during start should be a good enough solution as we generally don't expect etcd clusters to downgrade. As of etcd v3.5 it is not an officially supported feature.

For now posted as a "help wanted" issue, however if we cannot hit the timeline for 1.30 code freeze ([5th March](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-release/tree/master/releases/release-1.30#summary)) I would take it over so we don't miss. Still issue is simple enough that it can be quickly implemented.

/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted
/help

### Why is this needed?

Warn users about running on buggy etcd version

body:
### What happened?

BACKGROUND
I'm trying to create a small HA kubernetes cluster with 'kubeadm" following the topology "stacked control plane nodes" described here [1]. Considering I want to have 3 worker nodes, my infra looks as the following:
 - 6 nodes in total ( 3 control plane and 3 worker ).
 - All 6 nodes are within a GCP /28 subnet. In GCP, the first 2 and last 2 IPs of a subnet are unusable for the user. Meaning my cluster can run up to 12 nodes (16 - 2 - 2).
 - I'm also running an internal TCP Load Balancer with an internal IP within the same /28 subnet to distribute the traffic within the 3 control plane nodes, that leaves a total space of 11 nodes for the cluster.
 - Moving on, I decided to have a maximum number of pods per node of 64. For that, I have created a /20 secondary IPv4 range in the subnet, that I can divide into up to 16 /26 alias IP ranges for each node of my cluster.
 - I follow the same strategy for the services CIDR, I want a max of 64 per node, therefore I create a /20 secondary IPv4 range that I can later divide 16 times for each node as /26 alias Ip ranges.

When installing the cluster on the 1st control plane node, when I get to the step of running the command:
 $ sudo kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "192.168.0.7:6443" --upload-certs --pod-network-cidr "172.16.0.0/26" --service-cidr "172.16.4.0/26"

The thing is, the node subnet mask is not 24, but 28 ( see 2 bulletpoint in background ). I've tried several ways to change this value without success:
 - Via a now deprecated `kubeadm init` flag: --node-cidr-mask-size 28
 - Via providing a kubeadm configuration file [2] via the flag: --config
___

I would expect to be able to configure the Node CIDR Mask Size ( value other than 24 ) during the `kubeadm init` command step. Apparently, this was possible in the past with the flag `--node-cidr-mask-size`, see [3].

title: Enhancement: Improving control over parallel Execution parameter [--p] in E2E.
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I propose the addition of a new parameter, `--proc` to provide users with the ability to specify the number of parallel processes according to their requirements. 
This parameter would complement the existing parallel parameter `--p` which currently auto-detects the number of Ginkgo nodes based on CPU counts.
Link [here ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/conformance/image/run_e2e.sh#L60-L66)for reference.

### Why is this needed?

The necessity arises from the current challenge faced when encountering resource constraints during parallel execution.

For instance, consider a scenario where an E2E YAML file sets resource limits for CPU and memory. If a node with a high CPU count initiates parallel execution, it may lead to resource exhaustion due to the specified limits. Consequently, test failures may occur, disrupting the testing workflow and potentially delaying project timelines.

To mitigate this, users typically resort to manual adjustments of resource allocations within the E2E YAML file. By introducing the `--proc` parameter, users gain granular control over parallel execution, enabling them to align it with predefined resource constraints effectively.

This enhancement promotes efficient resource utilization and fosters more reliable testing outcomes across diverse infrastructure environments.

/sig testing

title: Daemonset RollingUpdate does not correctly count old non-ready pods towards MaxUnavailable budget
body:
### What happened?

Starting with a cluster of three nodes, with a healthy deamonset pod running on each, with `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable=1`.
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-7fmn7   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running   0          17s          
```

When performing three updates to the daemonset, each with some reason that prevents the new pods from becoming ready, I  ended up with zero ready pods.
```
kubectl get pods                                                                                                                                               
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-5sbf5   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-bswfc   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-jgdv7   0/1     Running   0          9s
```


### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that when I apply an update, and the new pods fail to become ready, when I apply a second update the "new" failing pods are replaced before considering any of the oldest healthy pods.
This is similar behavior to how Deployments work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a three node (or any count really) cluster, create this daemonset, which is just an nginx pod with a startup probe hitting port 80.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: demo-daemonset
  namespace: 
  labels:
    app: demo-daemonset
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo-daemonset
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo-daemonset
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          failureThreshold: 5
          periodSeconds: 3
```
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-7fmn7   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running   0          17s          
```

Update the startup probe port to something other than port 80, which should cause the pod to never become ready, and apply again.
```yaml
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8081
```
You can see the new unhealthy pod, and the generation of each pod
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running            0             5m41s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running            0             5m41s
demo-daemonset-zmqnj   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6 (46s ago)   4m59s

kubectl get pods -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,generation:.metadata.labels.pod-template-generation,ready:status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'
NAME                   generation   ready
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1            True
demo-daemonset-mflls   1            True
demo-daemonset-zmqnj   2            False
```

Repeat this process for as many nodes/pods as you have (2 more in this example), changing anything that would cause the pods to be recreated (in this case I just cycled the startup probe port a few times).
```yaml
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8082
```
```
kubectl get pods                                                                                                                                               
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-4rpgq   0/1     Running   0          3s
demo-daemonset-7wfxm   0/1     Running   0          3s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          6m27s

kubectl get pods -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,generation:.metadata.labels.pod-template-generation,ready:status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'
NAME                   generation   ready
demo-daemonset-4rpgq   3            False
demo-daemonset-7wfxm   3            False
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1            True
```

After the 2nd update, you can see that it has replaced both the 2nd generation pod (the one that was failing), and one of the first generation pods. Im now down to 1 out of 3, when I had specified `maxUnavailable=1`.

One more apply / update, and all generation 1 pods are gone, and all pods are unhealthy.
```

title: Make `fmt.Errorf` use `%w` to wrap error instead of `%v`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make it canonical to use `%w` for all `fmt.Errorf` to wrap error. If it's believed a good idea, we can add lint check.

### Why is this needed?

According to [fmt.Errorf doc](https://pkg.go.dev/fmt#Errorf), verb `%w` will make it return a new error wrapping the operand error, which allows using `errors.As()`. Many error [handling functions](https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.29.1/pkg/api/errors/errors.go#L546) in k8s rely on `errors.As()`. However, the majority of `fmt.Errorf` in current k8s code is using verb `%v`, which may lead to false assumption in using `errors.As()`.

There might be good reasons to use `%v` to abstract the implementation details as well, but it should be rare.

title: Move validation functions of Templates into staging
body:
### What would you like to be added?

It would be ideal to have the validation logic in staging so users of JobTemplate could check for validation errors and log an error.

I think that we would just need a function that returns the fieldErrors and that way we can reuse the same validation logic but also do a bit of validation when using JobTemplates.

### Why is this needed?

In the JobSet project, we are composing the JobTemplate in our JobSet spec. This works fine but we are having trouble validating the JobTemplate. We basically create it and the template can fail. 

We would like to have a way to validate the JobTemplate using the same rules that is in pkg/validation. It would be great if we had a function we could call as part of the API.

See https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/issues/422.

title: Persistent Thread and Memory Allocation by Kubelet Post-Workload
body:
### What happened?

`Kubelet` does not release threads and their associated memory allocations after handling high workloads, leading to inefficient resource usage and potential node performance degradation.

### What did you expect to happen?

Expected kubelet to free up threads and memory resources once the workload decreases, returning to baseline resource usage levels.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Deploy a set of pods with containers that have frequent readiness probes, simulating a high workload on kubelet.

- Monitor kubelet process resource usage (threads and memory) before, during, and after the workload using system monitoring tools.

- Observe resource usage after reducing the workload to verify if resources are released.

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue may lead to resource exhaustion and affect the overall performance of the Kubernetes node, especially in dynamic workload environments.

title: Allow disabling Kubelet Pods/containers log cleanup
body:
Log lifecycle management is part of Kubelet attributions. 

It is done [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/252e1d2dfee63e3165c4277ce1709d635df5132f/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L1267) and basically, when a Pod doesn't exists anymore it will remove any logs from the filesystem.

On some cases, the logs from the container runtime are not being shipped externally and there may be a need to disable this behavior (being the responsibility of the cluster admin to set some log rotation and cleanup). As an example, a Pod that is deleted by a bad actor will have all of its logs gone. Those lost logs may be required for a future forensics.

The request here is to add a flag/config on kubelet that allows the cluster admin to disable this cleanup, which means, when a Pod is deleted, no request to the container runtime will be made to remove its logs, skipping the `removeContainerLog` function call.

Thanks

/sig node
/kind feature

title: [APF] Separate Events requests from non-Events
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Adding separate `prioritylevel`s for Events to avoid resource competitions to non-event requests.

I currently think two ways of separation:

Option 1:

Create a new FS and PLC for events. The new FS will catch all events regardless of requestors. PLC will have a minimum `nominalConcurrencyShares`

| Name | Nominal Shares | Lendable | Borrowing Limit | Min Shares |
| ---- | -------------: | -------: | -----------------------: | --: |
| event |  5 |   100% | none | 0 |

Rules
```
  rules:
  - nonResourceRules:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups:
      - '*'
      clusterScope: true
      namespaces:
      - '*'
      resources:
      - events
      verbs:
      - '*'
    subjects:
    - group:
        name: '*'
      kind: Group
    - user:
        name: '*'
      kind: User
```

Option 2:

Create a mirror of existing FSs and PLCs for event counterparts

| Name | Nominal Shares | Lendable | Borrowing Limit | Min Shares |
| ---- | -------------: | -------: | -----------------------: | --: |
| node-high-events       |  5 |  100% | none | 0 |
| system-events          |  2 |  100% | none | 0 |
| workload-high-events   |  2 |  100% | none | 0 |
| workload-low-events    | 5 |  100% | none | 0 |
| global-default-events  |  2 |  100% | none | 0 |


The numbers of "Nominal Shares" need more thoughts to be more reasonable but they should be minimum with the hope to use borrowed concurrent shares. I am inclined to Option 1 for its simplicity. 

### Why is this needed?

In my tests that add a few hundreds of nodes to the cluster, I noticed if the machine that hosts `apiserver` & `etcd` is too small, `apiserver` can be easily stressed out and starts responding 429s and 504s (also, nodes became NotReady due to missing lease renews). However, in fact, the majority of the resources were consumed to serve event requests. If I removed events entirely, the cluster was able to survive the whole test more healthily. 

AIUI, event requests are less critical but voluminous so they likely compete currency shares with non-event requests when apiserver is under stress. It's more ideal to process Events when apiserver has free capacity.

To give a sense of competition, I observed POST requests of 3k non-event and 9.3k event from kubelet (also a few thousands from scheduler and controller-manager etc) in a test adding 200 nodes to a k8s cluster. Worth mentioning POST requests have to hit the ETCD so they are pretty expensive in terms of the duration occupying the concurrency shares as well as the machine resources.

Most importantly, event requests are resilient to temporary failures. For example, events are stored in client side up to [1000](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.29.1/tools/record/event.go#L43) before dropping. So it seems relatively safe to reject or throttle event requests.
